articles.text:
REGISTERED FOR

No. 549.

THE MAT-MAKERS AND THE HOUSE

OF COMMONS.
• Tan debate on Colonel BEEESFORD'S motion
on the employment of convict labour was very
interesting, and to those who take an interest
in the practical government of the country,
could not fail to be also very instructive. How to
employ our criminals most usefully for them-
selves and most beneficially for the general
community, is, in its very nature, a question
of great importance, and when it came up
for discussion in the House of Commons—an
assembly composed, for the most part, of
gentlemen practised in the disoussion of public
affairs, and in the presence of Heads of Depart-
ments who ought to be able to penetrate the
most difficult mysteries of Governments—we
had a right to expect that the subject would
be handled wisely and well; that, what was
uttered should smack of experience and
thoughtfulness, and that the conclusions come
to should evidence the power as well as the
will to carry out such reform as might be
proved necessary.
It would be pleasant to be able to say so
much of the debate in question; but it would
not be right to do this. Nearly everything
uttered was feeble, loose, and disjointed. Not
one of, the speakers seemed to possosa a firm
grasp of the subject. And although "facts"
of the ordinary questionable kind were flung
about abundantly enough, nobody pointed out
with sufficient distinctness the real source of
the mat-makers complaints, nor at all indicated
the way in which prison labour shall cease to
be offensive and injurious to working men.. •
The offence against the mat-makers is •plain
enough. They are a small body, a rather ill-
paid trade, not capable of bearing up sue-,
cessfullY against a severe competition; and
almost necessarily, so near to the dividing
line between honest independent labour
and the outlying wastes and jungles of
pauperism and crime, that an unfair competi-
tion from the prisons of the country might
easily starve them, and drive them and their
children hopelessly forth amongst the useless
and the lawless, in their turn to become State
competitors against other poor wretches still
struggling to live independent and honest
lives. There arc 6,000 of them, men, women,
and children, but these have been so added to
by workers in prisons—Wakefield notably—
that the competition is ruining them, and
that too, an unfair competition, which sells
the manufactured article at a little over the
east of raw material. They bought the goods
themselves to test the matter, and can produce
them and the. invoice in proof of what they
Say.

The loose statements made in reply to
Colonel BERESE'ORD prove the necessity for

inquiry—not altogether in the interest of the
mat-makers—they are clearly too insignificant
a body to call for the sympathy of legislators
or practical statesmen ; but as this question
has a visible connection with labour in all its
branches, it might have commanded more
attention than it did in the House of Commons.
And if there had been a few intelligent working
men in that assembly, it most certainly would
have commanded a fuller and more intelligent
consideration. Mr. KENNA.WAY'S speech was
a good thoughtful utterance in its way, but
it scarcely touched the question as it affects
the mat .makers. He was against an injudicious
competition with particular trades, Mat-
making, he thought, was taken to by
_heads of prisons in "despair." He thought
the question was one which needed further
ventilation; at present they were working, to
a great extent, in the dark. And this admis-
sion, more candid than encouraging, was con-
firmed by the whole course of the debate.
Mr. WATERHOUSE declared that there were
only 584 prisoners in Wakefield employed
on mat-making, which shows how clear
his views are on this subject, when he
can regard such a source of supply run-
ning out continually on a circumscribed
industry as too harmless to be interfered
with. Mr. COLLINS was of opinion that the
convicts should be made to support themselves
by their labour; an opinion in which all parties
are agreed. How to do this is the question;
and Mr. COLLINS had no suggestion of any
kind to make in reference to it. Mr. WHIT-
WELL, who is a manufacturer, and who
ought to know better, admitted that the
prison mats might be sold to the wholesale
dealer cheaper than those produced by free
labour; but they were not so put into the
retail market; a statement which in no way
alters the case favourably for the working
man, as it only means that the wholesale
buyer may get them cheaper, but that the
retail buyer does not. This statement, if true,
only makes the mess worse, but it can't be
correct, as diminished wholesale price inevi-
tably leads to reduced retail price. Mr
AKROYD, another manufacturer, is in favour
of the jail system, and sustains it and justifies
it by tho fact that the Yorkshire ladies sub-
scribed £6,000 to support an industrial home
where the laundry work of Wakefield and its
neighbourhood is taken in and executed.
possibly to the injury of many poor women,
but without the chance of their making their
grievances heard in Parliament, as it would
never do to call Parliamentary attention
to the case of a number of women whose
living was obtained from so humble an article
as the washing tub. Besides, the Member for
Halifax gave the superfluous assurance that in
America prison authorities encouraged industry
in the prisons of that country, as they regarded
idleness as a great cause of crime. He did not
say, however, whether they did this in the
same blundering manner in which it is done at
Wakefield, nor did he inform the House that in
the United States, competition in the labour
market is less severe than it is in England.
There, it adds to the sum total of the wealth of
the country, without displacing and ruining,
the independent honest worker, or without
forcing the free competitor into that compul-
sory idleness which he informs us is the parent
of so much crime.

Mr. BRUCE, however, was the most blunder-
ingly absurd. of all the speakers. How he

managed to get through some of the sentences
he gave utterenee to, without pulling up and
laughing at himself, is quite amazing. "In
Pentonville and Milbank, no doubt the trade
of mat-making, among others, was follow ed
but the object had been to find a multiplicity
of employments, in which prisoners might,
after their discharge, earn an honest liveli-
hood." It will not be necessary to read this
utterance of our Home Secretary twice to dis-
cover its folly, or to understand what little
wisdom is needed to do the business of Govern-
ment where only the interests of poor men
require to be attended to. Mr. lianoz clings
to mat-making, that the discharged prisoners
who learn it may get an honest living when
liberated. But it is clear that a small trade
like this, supplied extensively by the labour
of actual prisoners, cannot give a fair chance
of an honest livelihood to discharged criminals.
This is keeping the word of promise to the ear,
and breaking it to the hope, with a vengeance..
They might as well teach them to make leather
breeches, women's pattens, sedan chairs, or
any other obsolete articles as to instruct them
in a business confined to three thousand men,
half-idle already in consequence of prison com-
petition. This is not teaching a prisoner a
trade by which he may live when he becomes
a free man; it is rather teaching a trade by
which he cannot live, and which almost forces
on him the necessity of relapse and recommit-
ment. Well might Mr. KENNAWAY say that
this mode of employing criminals was resorted
to "almost in despair."
Nor is this policy rendered more endurable
by Mr. BRUCE'S other statement, that mat-
making and similar trades were taught because
many of the prisoners were only in for a short
time. In such cases they had better be em-
ployed in some way which would not render
their competition ruinous to a few thousand
pour people who have no protection from the
mistakes of prison officials, but in the common
sense and common sympathy of the masses of
the people—not always an effectual protection,
and certainly, whether effectual or not, always
painfully slow in its operation.
This question,whieli to working men is of very
great importance, served simply in the House
of Commons for a gentle display of oratorical
courtesy. Two or three mild verbal essays pro
and con, and then a drawn battle resolution and
amendment laid on the shelf—and the road to
ruin left open that the mat-makers may move
on to the end without let or hindrance. Can
Mr. GLADSTONE, as head of the Government,
know how much he loses in public confidence
by permitting in his subordinates such blun-
dering imbecility as that displayed by Mr.
BRUCE in this case? Has he, and have those
who act with him, come to the conclusion that
working men generally are half-blind idiots,
without any clear or definite conception as to
what injures or improves their condition as a
class? Or, are they foolish enough to go on
believing that the working men will continue
to support them even though they refuse to
deal wisely and justly with labour questions?
Working men, it must not be forgotten, do
not wish to have the criminals of the nation
kept without work. They have to toil hard
enough themselves, and they do not desire to
see scoundrelly law-breakers kept in idleness
at their expense. But they have a right to
expect that those who make .laws for the
country, that those who are paid for
governing the country, that men who have

to deal practically with difficult social
problems, shall tackle their work like men,
shall not ride off on personal and class
conveniences, leaving to injured working
men who have no true power in the State, the
right only of suffering and grumbling. They
have no right to bring prison work into inju-
rious competiton with free honest labour. They
should in the interest of the unhappy criminals
as well as in the interest of the general cow.
munity, give such diversity of instruction as
would enable liberated prisoners to drop into
a great variety of employments, and not to
overstock and ruin a few. For this purpose
they should classify the prisoners properly, and
so act as to prove that they really understand
what they are about. As things stand they
do the least service to the unhappy creatures
under their charge, and the largest amount of
injury to the trades they undertake to teach.
The mat-makers have a most substantial
ground of complaint, and. if some wise change
be not made, working men generally will have
to take the matter in hand, and compel suoh
a reformation of our prison system, as those
now in power have neither the common semi
nor the courage to set about.
ILLorn Arms.

articles.title: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT
articles.text:
THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT

ACT.

IN my letter which appeared in the BEE-
rlivE of the 6th inst., I advised the agricul-
tural labourers who asked my advice to
to " be careful to keep within the pale of the
law, as the Criminal Law Amendment Act
which was specially enacted against trades
unionists in towns, would be applied with
equal rigour against theinin the country."
Four days after writing the above I found
my anticipation in this respect fully- verified
in the columns Of the Daily Nolts, *WA con-
tained a report of the charge to the Cirandjnry
at the Warwickshire Quarter SesSions by the
Chairman, who is reported to have "explained
at length the Acts passed last Session with re-
spect to trades unions, and the punishment of
various offences, and observed that it was do.
sirable that it should be generally known that
there Acts are applicable to agricultural
as well as manufacturing districts," and
wound up his unseemingly outrageous
harangue, in true chairman of Quarter Ses-
sions style, by cautioning the agricultural
labourers against "hired demagogues,"
if anybody can tell us who they are.
In honourable and praiseworthy contras t to
this Warwickshire Squire stands the admi
rable charge to the Grand jury by Earl RADNOR
at the Wilts Quarter Sessions. His Lordship
directed the attention of the jury to the pro-
bable turn which the labourers' agitation will
take in that county, and observed, " For his
own part, he was bound to confess that ho saw
no reason why the labourer should be deprived
of his right respectfully to ask for an increase
in his wages. The wealth of the country had
greatly increased during the last few years,
and most classes had benefited by that increase,
and it was only reasonable that the labouring
classes should participate in that benefit the
same as any other class, and that they should
in a proper and becoming way endeavour to
reap a little benefit from the general weal. He
felt that a kind feeling between employer and
employed was essential to the well being of
both, and for that reason ho sincerely hoped
the question would be viewed in the light he
had suggested."

According to the report, it appears that the
foreman of the Grand jury, which in the
rural districts is chiefly composed of th o

squirearchy or "gentlemen farmers," objected
to his Lordship's remarks about the prosperity
of the country, and, to prove his ignorance
upon the subject, declared that the limy
could not agree with his Lordship
.that
the wealth of the country had geneially
increased." Whereupon Lord RADNOR
stated that "if the farmers are not so
thriving as they could wish, I can only say I
am sorry for it. I am. a landlord myself, and
shall be prepared to assist my tenants in
every way in my power. I will meet them
half way in order that the existing grievance
may be remedied." (Applause in the Court.)
A juror :—Thank you my lord; if the other
owners of property would but follow your
example, we should get on very well."
No doubt they might get on very well if
landlords and chairmen at Quarter Sessions
would advise conciliation "with an entire
absence of coercive measureS on either side,"
as advised by Lord RADNOR. But will the
"gentlemen farmers" and chairmen of Quarter
Sessions do this? With rare exceptions it is
to be feared they will pursue an opposite
Course, if we may judge from the opposi-
tion that has been shown to the agricultural
labourers' union; and, therefore, they must
be prepared for the same kind of
treatment which is dealt out to their
brother unionists in the different towns ; and
in order that they may know what that treat-
ment is, and what they have to expect by the
application of the Criminal Li* Amendment
Act, I will place before them the latest convic-
tion under this. infamous Act. The daily
papers report that an "elderly woman was
brought before the magistrates at Leeds on
Tuesday, the 9th inst., on a charge of intimi-
dation against the hands who had taken the
place of those on strike at the works of Messrs.
MA.RSIIALL, for calling out " black sheep, Sze.,"
and was sent to gaol for fourteen days without
the option of a fine." Now, the question to be
asked and answered is this :—ls the fact of a
woman having called out "black sheep" an
act of intimidation sufficient to justify the
magistrates in sending her to prison without
the option of a fine, and thereby attaching the
stigma of criminality to her for the remainder of
her life? By all means where acts of violence are
committed, punishment ought to follow, and
the leading trades unionists and their friends
have been among the first to advocate this.,
But the common law or ordinary statute law
is quite sufficient to deal with. cases of this
kind, or even intimidation where threatening
language and a Menacing attitude has clearly
been proved; and therefore there is no necessity
for any gioaid.l penal law which places it with-
in the Power of any miscreant to swear away
the liberty of his fellow workmen to curry
favour with an unscrupulous employer. The
magistrates are bound to send all those to
prison who are convicted
,under the Crimina
Law Amendment Act.; and although they
arc supposed to exorcise a discretionary
power up&i the nature of the evidence, the
working' of the Act has proved that both the
stipendiary and unpaid magistrates have
strained the Act to obtain convictions. This
fact was pointed out to Mr. BRUCE when the
members of the " Parliamentary Committee"
appointed by the Trades' Congress waited
upon him to urge the necessity for the
repeal of the Act. They brought be-
fore his notice, among others, the case of
tho illegal conviction of the mason at Bolton,
and the engineer at Hammersmith, and, as
might have been expected, he told the deputa-
tion that "the law had been misunderstood
and misapplied in these cases." What a
mockery to talk about the law being misapplied.
Why, it will never be anything else while it
remains on the otatuto book. But where is the
necessity of this Amt, which is specially
directed against trades unionists, while all !
other associated bodies of men are dealt with,
as all ought to be, under the ordinary or
common law? The fact is, the Criminal Law
Amendment Act is neither more or less than a
dangerous piece of net work, to catch and
brand with the stigma of criminality all those
trades unionists who may venture to offer any
remonstrance, or give any explanation to their
fellow workmen when any dispute occurs
between thorn and their employers. It is the
most oppressive R 1.14 unjust Act that ever

disgraced. the statute book of this country. I
do not believe that Lord CAIRNS and the
Lords who supported him in what they con-
sidered to be the amendment of the Act, had
any idea as to the base uses it would be
applied by unscrupulous employers.
Certainly no English gentleman would ever
sanction such a law who is fully acquainted with
the desires, the intentions, and the every day
practices of the great body of trades unionists.
I claim the right to speak with some authority
on this point, hiving had under me during the
last . thirty years in different parts of the
country from time to time, thousands of trades
unionists, and although I was never the man
to flatter them or pander to their feelings, I feel
bound to say that I never found any
difficulty
in dealing with these men, where reasonable
attention was paid to any suggestion or com-
plaint they had to make, and 1. always found
the common law strong enough to deal with
eases of assault or intimidation. Therefore I
hope the trades unionists will demand the total
repeal of the Criminal Law Amendment Act
as a piece of unjust special class
legislation
directed specially against them.
ALFRED A. WAITOr•
Brecon, April 15th.

CONTAGIOUS DISEASES BILL.

THE signature of HUMPHREY SANDWIVE
is a guarantee that the best statement is
made of a case advocated by him. He tells
us that the medical profession are our best
advisers as to legislative measures where
health and disease are concerned. But what are
we to do when" Doctors disagree?" In several
towns a very large majority of our medical
men condemn 'these Acts, as your own columns
have testified. Let us, however, assume that
the eradication of disease is the only object; vro
ought, as they say, to "go the whole hog,"
establish brothels under Government iaspeo-
Lion, and at the public cost, and hang every
prostitute who is not resident in one of them.
I am persuaded from medical testimony, the
disease is increased, and not diminished by the

QUESTIONS BY A POSITIVIST.
, _

NINTH QuESTioN,-7Can Mr. OWEN be con-
sidered "the greatest of social Reformers,'
when it is admitted that he adopted a funda-
mental error into his system, which " poisoned
the flow of truth at its source
ANSWEE.—This mistake of Mr. Owns, the
denia' of the highly important truth that man
has a power of self-government (which was
owing* to the Very defective state of mental
science, and which no one in his day was able
to correct), does not alter the fact that he. was
the discoverer of the knowledge of the causes
of evil and of good to man, in the formation of
character, in the production, and distribution
of wealth, and in social arrangements and pro-
ceedings in general; and that, therefore, he
was the first to point out the means by which
alone a system of effective social reform can be
realised; and that he. verified practically at
New Lanark, in a most admirable manner, the
irresistible, and to those who know only the
experience of old world education, the wonder-
ful power for good in the formation of character
which men will obtain by acquiring the know-
ledge of the causes of evil and of good to man,
and by acquiring also the enlightened goodness
which this knowledge alone can enable men to
attain. Without the intellectual and moral
character which cannot exist in the absence of
this knewledge, and without, the knowledge
which 15 necessary to enable societies to pro-
duce and distribute wealth beneficially fur all,
and in great superabundance, and to form
their social arrangements and institutions
beneficially fin. ell, the thoroughly reformed
state of society which alone can secure the
well-being and happiness of man, individually
and collectively, could never be realised. By
the fact that this great discovery—the greatest
discovery which ma,i can make—was made by
Mr. OWEN ; and that he was the first to ac-
quire the knowledge and the spirit, the intel-
,leotual and moral chara,oter, of the new system,
and. that he exhibited to the world a practical
example of the overwhelming new
,power
for good in education whieh man will
obtain by, acquiring this linowledge and
spirit; that he was the first to point
out the course which men must pursue to get
the knowledge, the true enlightenment, first,
and then., through this, to get the enlightened
goodness which the competent social reformer
must possess; and then, through these acquire-
ments, to carry out the practical measures
which are necessary for effectual social reform,
and to carry them out in the spirit of enlight-
ened*kindness to all, and without real injury
to any; he is shown, beyond question (beyond
question by any one who has the knowledge of
the subject which is necessary for the forming
of an intelligent opinion uponi.t), to have been
incomparably the greatest of Social'Reformers.
Others no doubt have had as much desire for
man's effectual improvement, in himself and in
his surroundings; but none have had the
knowledge necessary to enlighten this desire
and to make it practically efficient. That he
denied a highly important truth which the
world had rightly adopted, but which it had
partially falsified (the true part of the common
idea of free-will), and that he confounded, the

,
denial of this truth with the assertion of the
fundamental truth (relative to causation) which
the world had not known, and which in the
erroneous part of the common idea of free-will
it had denied, and the knowledge of which is
the first step towards the attainment of true
enlightenment ani of all the good which will
follow from it, was indeed a grave intellectual
defect, and was a most serious imperfection in
his great discovery, by which for a time its
brilliancy has been darkened. But when this
error is removed, with the exaggerated con-
clusions to which it leads, the truth remains
in all purity, unaffected by the temporary
adulteration with error to which it had been
subjected.

TENTH QUESTTON.-If you do not adopt
exactly the same principles as Mr. OWEN,
what right have you to appeal to Mr. OWEN'S
New Lanark experiment as an instance of
what true principles can effect? If the belie,
that man's character is entirely formed for him
has a tendency to cause men to be charitable
for differences of opinion or immoral continet
as it may be admitted it has; in proportion as
you modifiy this doctrine, and introduce some
element of free-will, do you not destroy or
weaken the moral influence of the nocessatian
doctrine.

ANSWER.—The moral influence of the neces-
sarian idea is beneficial so far only as that
idea is true—that is, so far as the truth rela-
tive to causation is asserted in that idea. It
is injurious so far as the. true part of the
.com-
mon idea of free-will is denied. The charit-
able feelings which result from the application
of the knowledge that man is the creature of
causation, when this is combined with, the
knowledge Of man's power of self-government,
are purely beneficial. By the fact that man
has a power of self-government we arc justified
in feeling displeased when that power is not
exerted as it should be. But by the fact that
man is the creature of causation—that there is
always a cause for his exerting or not exert-
ing his power of will effectively—we are re-
quired to Moderate our displeasure, and the
feeling of sympathy is excited within us with
which we look upon a person who is suffering
from bodily disease. Wrong doing is the
effect of mental disease. To have the
erroneous ideas and injurious habits of feeling
Which are the, cause of wrong doing, is to. be
mentally diseased. , And this
,is the effect of
the injurious influences of the existing system,
including of course the false ideas, the intel-
lectual disease, and the consequent injurious

feelings, the moral disease, upon which this
system is based. But where the mental
disease is not so excessive as to deprive the
patient of all power of self-government, there
is room for blame, although there is not the
justification of harsh and vindictive feelings
which is obtained from the erroneous part of
the common idea of free will, from the idea
that man is himself the primary or sole cause
of his character, Bco. If with the necessarians
we regard man as entirely destitute of power
of self-government, we are required, by this
idea to. feel the same charity towards him
which we feel for the insane. For the differ-
ence between sane and insane persons is, that
the sane have a power of self-government,
more or loss, Mit the insane, so far as they are
really insane, have no such power at all. And
by the correction of the necessarian idea the
wrong-doer is deprived of the justification of
wrong doing which is derived from the suppo-
sition that man has no power of self-govern-
ment.

It was by the practical application of the
true part of the. necessarian idea, and of the
knowledge of
,the causes of evil and of good to
man, that the good results obtained at Net
Lanark were realised. The injurious effects
of Mr.. OWEN'S denial of man's power of self-
government were imperceptible while he did
not publish this negative idea
.to the world—
except that he was himself misled by this
idea in his reasonings, and to some ex-
tent intellectually confused. If in his.
writings we substitute the assertion of
the truth relative to causation, which
was really the
,basia,of his views, for the denial
of man's power of self-government, wherever
ho introduces, this debial, and if we substi-
tate the properly qualified ideas of man's
moral responsibility; kto., which are come-

quent upon the union Of the tiiito truths, for
the entire denial of man's moral responsibility
which is consequent upon the denial of
.man's
power of self-government, (and. we may always
do so with propriety, for
,he considered the
denial and the assertion as mutually equiva-
lent), we thus remove the leading errors by
which his teaching was falsified. And when
we are able- to do this we may perceive the
other exaggerations which are consequent upon
these errofs. And it is precisely those parts
of Mr. OWEN'S ViEWS which were most ob-
jected . to, and which really were highly
objectionable, and which were the chief
obstacles to the success of his taachink; which
are thus removed. And by this change we
not only remove erroneous ideas, which are
powerful causes of evil, but we substitute
_for,
them true ideas which will bepowqrful causes
of good. And by this, of coarse, we increase
, essentially the ofticacy. for good of the true.
-parts of the "New Views." And thus, ut
last, we find .ourselves in possession of the
new knowledge, in all purity, which alone can
enable man to reform- himself and his social
world 'effectually,. and to realise a state of
.permanent and ever increasing excellence and
high happiness over the. earth; and which
most certainly will in due time Cause. this
great consummation to be realised.

HENRY TILIVIS.

articles.text:
TIIE DuAinnts.

A meeting of assistants in the hosiery and
drapery trades was held on Monday last at Mr. W.
J. Pile's shirt factory, 71, Park-street, Camden-
town, for the purpose of considering the best
means of promoting the early closing movement
in this district. It was resolved that an association
be formed, to be called the "North-West London
Early Closing Association," to include all retail
trades. The attendance was large, and after some
discussion it was resolved that the meeting be
adjourned until Monday next, when a committee
and other officers will be appointed to carry on the
business of this association. The object is to
secure; a general closing at 9 p.m., Saturdays
excepted, in all trades; and to obtain for the
assistants the benefit of the Bank Holiday Act.

LEEDS.
THE FLAX STRIKE.

A mass meeting of operatives, to take into con-
sideration the present position of the flax strike,
was held on flolbeck Moor on Saturday afternoon.
About 2,500 or 3,000 persons were present, mainly
comprised of men and youths. Mr. William
Kendall presided.
The first resolution put to the meeting pledged
flax operatives of Holbeck to remain firm to the
nine hours demand, and to accept no compromise
in the shape of increased wages. It was proposed
by Mr. Jas. Higgins, seconded by Mr. Cunningham
and supported by Mr. B. Wrigley (mechanic).
_ _ _ _

Mr. Luke Hope moved the next resolution,
which pledged those workmen present of all other
trades to support the fhx operatives by all the
legitimate means in their power. His remarks
were frequently applauded.
Two delegates from Newcastle next spoke in
support of the resolution. The first who addressed
the meeting spoke against the employment of
women in factories, saying he supposed it was be-
cause the men did not got sufficient wages.
The remainder of the speech was to the effect
that by holding out, with the assistance of other
trades, they would be enabled to force the fifty-four
hours terms from the largo firm, and that not only
would reduced hours be obtained, but ultimately
increased wages. The resolution was passed, as
the other, unanimously. A collection was made
on the ground, and the proceedings shortly after-
wards terminated.

TRH TAILORS.

The Leeds Branch of the Amalgamated Society
of Journeymen Tailors presented a: new time bill
to their employers in January last, showing that
they required an advance of about 10 per cent, on
the present list of prices. After several meetings
between the employers and their workmen, the
following firms acceded to the wishes of the men
—namely, Messrs. J. W. Smith and Son, Gibbons
and Clawler, T. Headland and Son, and Smalpage,
Cowlam, and Co.

NOTTINGHAM.
TUE orrataTivn STONE MASONS.

A meeting was hold on April Sth, at the Oliver
Cromwell, Nottingham, when the following reso-
lutions were unanimously agreed to :—That wo
abide by our moderate and reasonable request of
one halfpenny per hour extra, and tlua fifty-four
hours per week. And we view with regret the
course adopted by some of the employers, as it
leaves but one path for us to pursue with honour
to ourselves, and consistent with the dignity of
labour; and unless those employers accede to our
request before the Ist of May, we shall be obliged
to suspend work on that date in those firms that
offer an objection to our small request.

MIDDLETON.
STRIKE Ok SMALLWARE WEAVERS.

A strike took place on Saturday at several of the
sraallware Weaving establishments in Middleton in
consequence of the masters refusing to pay piece
prices instead of standing wages. In the evening a
meeting of hands was held, and there was a nume-
rous attendance. Delegates from Manchester,
Derby, Congleton, and Leigh delivered addresses
in favour of bolding out against the masters. The
unions have promised 10s, week per Iteß4 for All

adult turnouts, and Is. a head for each child under
ten years of age, so long as the strike continues.
One large firm in the neighbourhood pays piece
prices.

On Monday morning a largo number of the turn-
outs assembled in the Market Place, Middleton, and
the following resolution was carried unanimously:
—"We, the smallware weavers of Middleton, here-
by enter our protest against the present pernicious
weekly wage system, and in order to protect the
honourable employer, as well as to establish a
uniform rate of payment, we claim to be paid in.
future in accordance with the recognised list now
in operation at Mr. Jackson's establishment, and
resolve not to resume wozk until such list has been
conceded."

THE BUILDING TRADES.

At a meeting of carpenters and bricklayers held
at the Sun Inn, High-street, Maidstone, on
Saturday evening, April 13th, 1872, Mr. Tomlin
in the chair, and Mr. Horsecroft in the vice-chair,
to hear the reply of the employers after the con-
ference with the deputation, the chairman
said:—

1314.0 TITER WOIRKMBN,—I am proud to say
I have something far more cheering to tell you
this evening than on any former occasion; I will
tell you at once—it is a step in the right direc-
tion. He then read the reply of the employers,
the first part of which was received with great
attention, but having come to that part were it
states the men were to have no breakfast-time in
winter, much dissent was expressed by the meet-
ing; they said they would never allow the world
to call them" no break fast Maidstoners." Along
discussion ensued with reference to the reply.
Ultimately the following resolution was moved,
seconded and adopted :—" That this meeting,
having heard the offer made by the employers to
our memorial and code of working rules after the
conference with the deputation, think it a step in
the right direction; but it is most unsatisfactory,
as some six years ago we had a struggle of six
weeks' duration for the very amount per hour they
now offer, and cannot think of accepting anything
less than 7d. per hour all the year through, 54
hours to constitute a week's work from the second
Monday in February to the second Monday in
November, and 60} hours from the second Monday
in November to the second Monday in February;
and further we cannot think of deviating from the
general tenor of the code of working rules." The
meeting then desired the committee to forward
this resolution to the employers, and concluded
with a vote of thanks to the chairman and vice-
chairman.

April 12th, 1872.

Stn,—At a meeting of master builders, hold at
the Bell Hotel this evening, the following resolu-
tions were adopted :

"Firstly, that on and after the Ist day of July,
the standard wages of bricklayers and capenters of
this town be 6id. per hour."
"Secondly, the full time of 561 hours to com-
mence on the second Monday in February, and
terminate tho second Monday in November; and
that short time of 501 hours commence on the
second Monday in November, and terminate the
second Monday in February, beginning at 7.30
a.m., having breakfast previous to commencing
work, and half an hour only to dinner."
"Lastly, that all other existing regulations re-
main unaltered."

I am, Sir, yours truly,
J. S. ANSCOMII, Chairman.
Mr. Tomlin, Sun Inn, Maidstone.

]3IThJING}IMI,

ARBITRATION IN TUB BUILDING TRADES.

At Birmingham, on Friday evening, the Court
of Arbitration, to settle the questions in dispute
between the masters and operatives in the building
trades—the carpenters and joiners, the plasterers,
and labourers—was resumed in the Grand Jury
Room at the Public Offices, !Dloor-street, Mr.
Rupert Kettle being the arbitrator. The Court
was adjourned from Monday last in order that the
arbitrator might consider his decision upon the
question of "time," the co ntention being then for
63 hours on the part of the men, and 54 hours by
the masters. Upon this point the arbitrator
delivered his decision as follows

"I may be permitted to explain, in a few words,
the circumstances under which I reserved iny de-
cision upon the proposition submitted to me at our
last meeting. Hitherto, in settling disputes in the
building trine, it has been my practice to consider
the whole of the matters in dispute before arriving
at a final decision; and also, when it is practicable,
by the same settiement to embrace all the branches
of the trade in one uniform system. There are
many obvious :advantages in taking this course in

a trade where time and the rate of wages act and
react upon each other. It sometimes has happened
that a final and satisfactory bargain has been the
result of a concession by one party as to one point,
and of the other party as to another point. In the
case before me it has been thought advisable to have
the hours of work settled quite independently of any
other matter in difference, and that at an arbitra-
tion meeting where only three branches of the
trade—the carpenters, the plasterers, and the
labourers—are represented, the other branches
not having expressed, by notice under the rules,
any desire to alter the hours of work. Now, so
far as the labourers are concerned, it is positively
necessary their hours should be contemporary
with each and all other branches. Although the
discussion before me here had given me a clear
impression of what would be substantially just in
in the matter before me, still I thought it right,
having regard to the position of all parties, to con•
eider what would be the complete efftct upon the
convenience of trade of any judgment I might give,
and for that purpose I reserved my decision for
further consideration. The single question we
met on Monday to consider was—What shall be
the hours in the branches of the building trade
which have given the notice? shall they be reduced
from 56/, as they stand at present, to 60i, as
claimed ? I need not recapitulate the arguments
which took place, or our ineffectual attempts to
make some compromise. They have been pub-
lished, and will be remembered. It was ultimately
left for me to decide whether the 56i hours should
be retained—whether they should be reduced to
50/, or whether any intermediate number should
be determined upon. In deciding this question I
have not only to consider the desires of the parties
in contention before me, but the combined inter eat
of both, so as not to disturb their trade and check
the demand for building. I have come to the
conclusion that, although from what has happened in
this town as elsewhere, customers way be disposed
to accept the results of what is called the nine
hours movement, they would not at present
willingly enter into bargains based upon still
shorter hours. I therefore, as much in the interest
of workman as of employer, decide that an
average of nine hours a day, that is 54 hours,
be the working week. This does not apply to the
three winter months."

The question being so far settled, the next point
was how the hours of labour should be arranged,
and whether the reduction should be taken off in
the morning or evening.
Mr. Loughton, for the carpenters, argued for the
settlement at six o'clock in the morning till five at
night, and from six till one on Saturdays.
The masters were in favour of from half-past
six a.m. till half-past five p.m. _ _

The operative plasterers contended for fixing the
hours the same as the carpenters and joiners.

On the question of payment they demanded 71d.

per hour.
Mr. Holmes thought qd. per hour was a fair
pike.

After somo discussion, the parties, at the sug-
gestion of the Arbitrator, retired to talk the
matter over, and eventually Mr. Holmes said, on
the part of the masters, that ho was prepared to
offer 7d. per hour, the arrangement to remain
unaffocted for two years.

Mr. Davison, the secretary, stated the men's
demand to be, "All overtime made at the request
of the employer, between 7 p.m. and 6 a.m. on
the first five working days, and after 12.30 p.m.
on Saturday, to be paid time and a half; Sunday
and Christmas Day double time." This point was
also allowed to stand over, it being almost
mutually agreed on.
On the question of payment of wages, both
parties agreed to the rule at present in existence,
namely, payment either on the works or at the
office not later than ten minutes past one o'clock
on the Saturday in each week.
The rule relating to " distance " was a sub-
ject for considerable discussion. The men
demanded a uniform rate, and 2s. per week was
ultimately agreed upon; but at the suggestion of
the Arbitrator, who said that his experience led
him to believe that the payment of railway fares
was best left an open question, that portion of the
rule was not pressed.

articles.title: NOTTINGHAM.
articles.text:
NOTTINGHAM.

MEETING OP FIIA3IEWORK KNITTERS.

On Monday morning a meeting of the shirt and
drawer branches of the trade was held in the
Mission Hall, off Broad-street, to consider the
Proposals made to the moo by the Board of Arbi-
tration. Mr. T. West, of Nottingham, presided,
and there were also present a large number of
workmen. The Chairman said it was necessary
in this struggle that the men should be thoroughly
united, and if they were united they must make
some impression on their employers.
Mr. Plumb stated that the managing committee
attended a meeting of the board on Thursday,
when some of the employers commented very
strongly on the workmen's proposals—he thought
they called it an impudent statement. He ex-
cused that remark, however, because during the
whole of his experience through life he never
knew any (Nat by down-trodden people to have
their rights to be anything else but impudence in
the opinion of the masters. The employers said

this thing had lasted so long that they could not
think of altering it. Mr. Hill told them their
proposals could not be entertained at all, and that
merchants would not buy the goods owing to the
high price which they would have to place upon
them. He (the speaker) replied that at the present
rate of pay the trade must go down, because there
was an insufficient number of men now at work
to produce the goods required, and those who were
in were seeking to get out. The masters said i f
the men would cross out the words "no charges,'
they might try to entertain the question. With
regard to the masters' inability to pay the prices,
he asked them to try their hands at making a dozen
of goods themselves, and he had no doubt if they did
so they would hurry back to the meeting and re-
commend the prices to be given, lie also told them
that if they could not elevate the branch the best
way would be to do away with it as speedily as
possible. lie then condemned the system of charges
for frames. He also commented upon the fact that
owners of machines put their men to work when
they knew there was only half work for them;
and, in conclusion, assured them that he told the
masters the men would not leave their present

position.
Mr. Bunting next addressed the meeting, and
said it was time tho accursed system of frame-
rents was done away with. He entered into a
calculation with regard to the earnings of work-
men in the branch, irom which it appeared that
the average earnings was las. 9d. per week; from
that amount there must be deducted 3s. Bd. torrent,
oil, light, and winding, which left 12s. Id. He need
not say that this meant starvation. Having re-
marked that winders got, within 2s. Id., the same
amount per week as workmen in the branch, ho
said what they asked for was an average of 16s. 6d.
per man. After some further observations, be
moved—

"That it is the opinion of this meeting that the
new statement placed before the Board of Arbitra-
tion was reasonable and just, and that we could
not, according to our present average, accept any
reduction on that list.

Mr. Plumb seconded the motion, which was
carried amid much cheering.

Mr. D. W. Heath, who was received with ap-
plause, in speaking with regard to the previous
resolution, said if they had made up their minds
that their list was a proper one, they could affirm
at a large meeting like this that their demands
were reasonable and just. When they send a large
number of men to Parliament pledged to the views
of Pazliarnent they mean to win for themselves a
great and glorious victory. (Loud cheers.) After
speaking of the Masters and Servants Bill, and
the Strike Act, the treatment of which showed,
he said, the want of labour representatives in the
House, ho referred to the Board of Arbitration,
and said that Board seemed to afford an opportu-
nity for one master to get to know what another
was selling his goods at, but as the workmen were,
to some extent, members of it, they would have to
go there again. He accordingly moved that the
Managing Committee have another interview with
the Board of Arbitration.

The resolution was seconded by a gentleman on
the platform, who remarked that the alteration
they sought for had been effected in Scotland.
The Chairman, in putting the motion, dissented
from Mr. Heath's views on arbitration with re-
gard to the lace trade. The Board of Arbitration
in the lace trade had, he thought, done good.
The resolution was carried, and the proceedings,
which had been conducted with the greatest en-
thusiasm and unanimity, were brought to a close.

articles.title: MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWS.
articles.text:
MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWS.

MinntxToNr.-t—A meeting of silk weavers was
held at Middleton on Saturday night to receive the
report of delegates to the masters of the district to
obtain their consent to an increase of about 71 per
cent. upon certain classes of goods. The delegates
reported that fourteen concerns in Manchester had
been visited, four in Middleton, four in Leigh,
four in Westhoughton, and several in Patricroft,
and that the general feeling was against making
any concession. A proposition to form a co-opera-
tive silk-manufacturing company in Middleton
was made, and was agreed to unanimously. The
meeting was adjourned for a week.
WEsTwoon.—The dispute of the quarrymen in
this district has at length come to an end, all the
employers having conceded the terms asked for.
SkiEFFIELD.—The dispute in the razor trade has
been referred to a conference of masters and
men.

KIRKCALDY.—The strike of fioorcloth workers
has been brought to a close by a compromise,
stipulating that the fifty-four hours should come
into operation forthwith, and that an advance of
wages should a lso taiga place.
SirrilmnounNv.—On Monday morning about a
hundred bricktnakers struck work. They were
engaged at three-and-sixpence per thousand, and

a fortnight ago the masters gave an advance of a
Penny. On Tuesday morning the gangs de-
manded twopence more, which the masters eon-
ceded conditionally on the market remaining at its
present height, and the men leaving sixpence in
hand as " pence:money." This was refused and the
men struck.

MANCHESTER.—The masters builders have deter-
mined to give the bricklayers' labourers 51d. an
• honr on and after the 15th June next. The masons'
labourers are also agitating for an advance.
At a meeting of the Manchester and Salford
Builders' Clerks' Association, held on Tuesday
• evening at the Hare and Hounds Hotel, Shudehill,
it was resolved that a memorial should be presented
to the master builders of Manchester, and the
neighbourhood, asking that the working hours of
'clerks might be from 8.30 a.m. to 5.30 p.m., with
the usual interval for dinner. The present work-
ing hours were complained of as being excessively
long; and in the memorial which was adopted the
masters were reminded that the clerks' occupation
was a sedentary one, and "well known to be any-
thing but conducive to health."
BRIDGEWATER.—The brickmakers have formed
a union, and will open a strike for an advance of

wages.
HARTLEPOOL. The stonemasons have just
entered upon a strike for the reduction of the
hours of work, to the extent of nearly ten hours
per week. Up to the present time, the men, who
number fully two hundred, have been in the habit
of working from 6 a.m. to 5.30 p.m., which,
allowing for half a day off on Saturday, made an
aggregate of 561 hours per week. The object of
their strike is to institute a commencement of
labour at 7 a.m. and cessation at p.m., which
would reduce the week's work to forty-seven
hours, at the same rate of wages hitherto paid—
viz., 30s. weekly. The masters resist this
proposal, although some of their number are
willing to shorten the day's work by half an hour
each day and increase the wages to 335. weekly;
but the men still hold out for the full concession
of their demands.
LEEDS.—The bricklayers, who at present receive
7d. an hour, resolved, at a meeting held on Wed-
nesday, in the Temperance Hall, St. Peter-street,
to demand an addtional id. per hour. About 300
were present at the meeting, which was composed
of,both society and non-society men. A deputation
was, appointed to wait upon the masters.
The shoemakers' dispute, which for more than a
fortnight has existed in Leeds between the rivetters
and finishers in the shoe trade and their employers'
is now amicably settled by the masters having
made concessions amounting to an advance of more
than 20 per coat. upon the wages previously p aid
LEICESTER.—The carpenters' strike continues
A meeting of the amalgamated unions of the Car-
penters' Society of Mancheeter and Bristol has been
held at Leicester on behalf of them, with the object
of bringing about a settlement. As they consider
the offer of the masters, of an advance of -id. per
hour from June Ist to be fair and honourable, 90 per
cent: of the masters have resolved to adhere to their
offer; They are satisfactorily filling up vacancies,
and only thirty masters have conceded the advance
of id., and the nine hours movement;
Wanntsurrosr.--In December last, the carpen-
ters and joiners gave the requisite notices for a
slight advance in wages and curtailment of work-
ing time. Certain rules have now been agreed
upon between them and their employers.
MACCLESFIELD. —The bricklayers have given a
very short notice to their employers for an altera-
tion in the leaving off time on Saturdays, which
they wish to be 12 o'clock. They have also given
notice for a rise of 6d. a day in their wages, to
commence on Ist June next.
FOREST OP DEAN.—On Saturday evening Mr.
Halliday, president of the Amalgamated Society of
Miners, addressed a large meeting of Forest of
Dean colliers, miners, and iron-workers at Cinder-
ford. He urged the establishment of conciliatory
relations between masters and men. A resolution
thanking the Government for the Mines Regulation
Bill was unanimously passed.
Bovrosi.—The letter carriers of Bolton have
addressed a memorial to the Postmaster-General
praying for an advance of wages. They state that
it is nearly 20 years since the present scale of re-
muneration was fixed, which is 16s. per week for
the first year, and an advance of 6d. per week for
each succeeding year, until tho maximum of 20s.
is attainel. They ask that the scale may in future
Commence at 205., and advance Is. per week per
year until 255. is reached.

Good value for money is desired by all, but with

articles.title: LONDON RAILWAY SERVANTS.
articles.text:
LONDON RAILWAY SERVANTS.

MEETING OF LONDON, CHATHAM, AND
DOVER MEN.
A numerously .attended meeting of the employes
in the Metropolitan District of the London, Chat-
ham, and Dover Railway, took place on Sunday
evening at the Imperial Hotel, Southwarkestreet,
at which Dr. Baxter Langley presided. There
were several mon from other lines also present.
The meeting was called to discuss the course to
be taken in consequence of the non-receipt of any
reply to a memorial which was sent in to the direc-
tors some weeks ago. The Chairman said he
thought the men on this lino of railway had fair
ground for complaint, inasmuch as the memorial
which contained nothing unreasonable, had been
submitted to the directors and also to the manager,
and there had been a duputation to the manager,
who had hoped the memorial would be taken into
consideration and its prayer granted; I but a long
time had elapsed, and nothing had been done. He
wanted them to consider this question not alone
their own case, but the case of railway servants
over the whole country. A society had long been
contemplated among railway men to make six days
to be considered a week and ten hours a day, more
particularly with regard to overtime. An execu-
tive Council was appointed, of which he was
chairman, and it was proposed to hold a general
delegate meeting in June next, which, considering
the extent of the railway interest, would probably
be one of the most influential meetings of the kind
ever held, as the class to be represented was
a most important one, and one in which the
public were most interested. Railway men wore
above the average for intelligence, and he would
venture to Bay that if they combined together, they
would have a union fir exceeding any other in
existence. What he would suggest would be to
form in this locality a branch of the Amalgamated
Society of Railway Servants, which had for its
object the reduction of the hours of labour, pay-
ment for Sunday work, and other advantages. He
hoped there would be no disposition to show any
party feeling in this matter, and that when one
man was asked to join in this cause, he should not
say that as his companion was only a shunter or in
some inferior station, ikce, he did not care to
associate with him. They must act as brothers—
man to man—and combine together all branches
of the service. There must be no pride, no suspicion
no distrust. Entering more largely into the
economical view of the question, the chairman
warned his audience against too freely accepting
overtime, on the ground that it would be more to
their advantage to let other men in who, if they
remained out, might reduce the price of labour.
Further he pressed upon them the necessity for
leisure, in order that they might learn and study
either from printed books or from the great book
of Nature which was open to all, and in this he
was certain that they would not only be promoting
their own interest and happiness, but those of the
great nation to which they all belonged.
A member of the Great Western, at Paddington,
said he was pleased at seeing so many railway
men present, and he trusted they were all earnest
in the object they had met for, shortening the
hours of labour. He was greatly pleased with the
address of the Chairman, and so had they been at
Paddington, where a meeting would be held again
that night. At Paddington they had presented a
memorial, and as no answer had been returned in
a fortnight, they again made application, and were
answered that it was under consideration, and had
not been forgotten ; but on the previous Thursday
a notice was issued calling a meeting for that
night, which was headed " Five months, and still
no answer." Whether it was this notice that
stirred the management into action, or what, he did
not know, but it had the effect of procuring them
an interview, and although all their requirements
were not conceded, still those that had been were
important. [The speaker then described the altera-
tions in the time that had been made, which will be
found in the report of the Paddington meeting below.]
In conclusion he said he should advise the men
not to rest satisfied until they were raid like other
labourers for six days in the week. Omnibusmen,
postmen, arid even the soldiers were paid for their
Sunday labour, and why should not railwaymen
have the same i Ile advised them to join the
Amalgamated Society. He believed the time was
not far distant when they would all unite and go
through life with a good opinion and a dependence
one on another, and when the railway men would
be looked upon the same as any other class.
(Hear, hear.)
The chairman said they had hero a practical
grievance, as nothing had come out of the memo-
rial that had been sent in, and this meeting should
be made use of to again bring under the notice of
the management that they desired an answer to
their memorial, and if a proposition, which he
believed was about to be put to the meeting, were

adopted, it would probably have the effect of
waking them up. (Laughter and cheers.)
The following motion was then adopted unani-
mously.
"That this meeting of railway employes of the
London District uf the London and Chatham and
Dover Railway, in the metropolitan district, re-
grets that the manager has not been in a position
to give any reply to the memorial sent in to him
in February last, and respectfully urges that he
should again bring the matter under the attention
of the directors."

A discussion then took place as to 'the most
desirable way of presenting this to the manager.
Eventually the chairman was asked if he would
kindly do so, to which he readily consented,
humorously adding "they could not spot him,"
and trusting that this application would be more
successful than the previous one.
A vote of thanks to the chairman closed the pro-
ceedings.

articles.title: MEETING OF GREAT WESTERN MEN.
articles.text:
MEETING OF GREAT WESTERN MEN.

On the same evening (Sunday), a large gather-
ing of the employes on the Great Western Rail-
way, also took place at the Red Lion, Harrow-
road, under the chairmanship of Dr. Baxter
Langley, when the following concessions by
the directors, in answer to. a memorial addressed
to them some months since were announced:
Passenger Porters :—The wages of the porters
to be as at present, viz., 175., 18s., and
193. per week. The hours of duty to be
twelve hours per day, with one and a half hour
for meals; Sunday work to be kept down as much
as possible, but to form part of the week's work.
Overtime to be based on seven days in the week,
at the rate of ten hours per day. Men on night
duty to receive Is. per week in addition to the
wages as per scale. Any man working two hours
or more per day between twelve midnight and
five a.m. to receive the extra pay for night duty.
Under the authority of the superintendent, to be
specially given in each case, the men may be
allowed to use a portion of the old clothes to
repair other garments. Porters working as
guards to receive overcoats when on guard's duty.
Signalmen: The pay to be for seven days per
week, but the men to be relieved as much as
possible of Sunday work. Policemen: The hours
of duty to be the same as for the porters. Goods
Guards: The present scale for the pay and pro-
motion of goods gnarls to remain in force. The
working day to consist of about ten hours, and
the week of about sixty hours, to include a
reasonable time during which the men may be
engaged before the departure and after the arrival
of the trains. Sunday duty to be limited as far
us possible, and, if exceeding the period of
above sixty hours per week, to be paid for
as overtime. The time and overtime to be
calculated by the booked time for the trains, work-
ing service book, and not on the time men are
actually on their journey. Any overtime in extreme
cases beyond the booked time, arising from acci-
dents or other special and unavoidable causes
beyond the control of the men, to be dealt with
specially on the merits of each case by the super-
intendent of the division. Goods Porters—The day
to consist of twelve hours, less one and a half hour
for meals, at intervals as convenient as possible,
according to the work, making the net working
time ten hours per day, or about sixty hours per
week. No more men to be on duty on Sunday
than are absolutely required by the necessities of
the traffic. Payment to be made as per clause 3.
The wages to bo calculated at the rate of six days
per week, Sunday work to be paid fur as overtime.
The present scale of st ages to continue in force,
viz.—Porters, Ist year, 18s. per week; 2nd year,
19s. per week; 3rd year, 20s. per week. The
wa,,es of the other grades to be as at present.
That overtime be paid as at present. Men
on night duty to receive is. per night in
addition to the wages as per scale. Any man
working two hours or more between midnight and
five a.m. to receive the extra pay for night duty.
Passenger Guards—The working of the short

train guards to be revised, and the time as far as I
possible equalised between the men. Sunday duty
to be reduced as far as possible, and if a guard is
brought on more than two Sundays a mouth, the
day to be paid for as overtime.
The speeches delivered by the representatives of
the several departments, while indicating a readi-
ness to accept the above concessions, exhibited a
feeling of great dissatisfaction on the part of the
men generally at the persistence of the directors in
not allowing for the work of the seventh day.
The Chairman enlarged upon this point, and
told his hearers that the great hope for the redress
of their grievances lay in the establishment of the
amalgamated union of railway servants, which was
now in course of formation. Having advised the
men to adopt the concessions as far as they went,
he referred in sarcastic terms to the proviso made
by the directors with respect to the retention of the

men's old clothes, and suggested, amidst cheering
mingled with laughter, that the Company had
better have a central depot in Petticoat-lane for
the sale of their servants' worn-out garments. A
resolution expressing regret that the directors had
not conceded the terms of the men, but at the
same time accepting for the present the concessions
enumerated, was agreed to unanimously.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

MIGRATION PROM THE AGRICULTURAL TO THE
MANUFACTURING D ISTUICTS.—The Rev. Canon
Girdlestone states that Captain Pali; the chief
constable of Manchester, who a faw weeks ago
recruited in North Devon 60 fine young men for

his force, has forwarded to him a letter, of which
a copy is given below. The Canon writes:—
"The men of the south, it is very true, when they

migrate northwards, cannot at first work beside
northera-bred men. But to use the words of a
correspondent of mine in Yorkshire, to whom I
have already sent many men, When, instead of
kettle broth, Devonshire men have had three
months' Yorkshire beef in their bellies, they can
work as well as a Yorkshireman."—" Newcastle-
on-Tyne, April 5, 1872.—Sir,—Will you kindly
inform Canon Girdlestone that he will be con-
ferring a great benefit on the poor people of
Dorset, Devon, Wilts, and Cs,ruwall, &c., if he
could send men hero in batches; for from the
Tyne to the Tees, especially on the two rivers, not
less than 5,000 men could find employment at
labourers' work at wages averaging from 18s. to
255. per week. I may tell you that the farm
labourers in Northumberland have just got their
wages raised from 18s. to 225. per week, with free
house, free coal, potatoes free, and three bolls of
wheat, and most of them nine hours per day,
with 6d. per hour for extra time, and half holidays
on Saturdays. I don't think many of the SJuth
Country men could get so much here for formwork,
for Northumberland men are tall, smart men,
very powerful, well educated, and the finest
countrymen I have seen in England. Carters in
this town get 255. per week. lam certain that
5,000 men could be absorbed in about three
mouths. The collieries, ironworks, &c., are so
busy that men cannot be got, and it is a sin to
allow Euglishmen in the south to emigrate from
their country whoa work can be found them hero
at good wages. Our chief Constable here is also
in want of policemen, and so are all the forces
about here. I don't know the Canon's address, and
am, therefore, obliged to trouble you, and will feel
obliged by your forwarding this.—l am, air, yours
faithfully, —. Captain Palma, chief, constable,
Manchester."

AGITA.TION IN DOILSETSIIIItE.—The agricultural
strike has at last extended to Dorset, and in the

Alabama Arbitration presented on Monday to
the Geneva Tribunal by the .British Govern.
meat was issued from the Foreign-office. The
Case discusses at considerable length the
claims put forth by the United Statea Govern-
ment, and maintains that the estimates of
losses, publics and private, presented by that
Government are " so 'loose and unsatisfactory,
and so plainly excessive in amount,
that they cannot .be accepted, even as
furnishing a prima fade basis of calcula-
tion." The consequences, which would result
to neutral Powers, Were the views .to be
sanctioned which the United States set up in
their claims for indirect damages, are considered
as very serious, For the first time in history,
the British Government helieves,it has been

neutral Government, is to be made the founda-

practice.

THE CRIMINAL LAW AMEND-
MENT ACT.

DEMONSTRATION OF TRADE SOCIETIES
• AT OLDHAM.

A. demonstration of trade societies, for the pur-
pose of protesting ag,ainst the Criminal Law
Amendment Act, and for agitating in favour of
the 54 hours movement, was held at Oldham on
Saturday.. The main feature of the demonstration
was a procession, consisting of representatives from
the following societies :—The Spindle and Flyer
Makers, the Operative Spinners of Oldham (two
branches), Chadderton, Hollinwood, Shaw and
Crompton, Lees, Middleton, and Royton ; the
Fustian Cutters, Amalgamated Engineers (four
branches), House Painters, Tailors, Bricklayers,
Carpenters and Joiners, Old Smiths, Skipmakers,
Hatters, Cordwainers, Printers, Coachbuilders,
Amalgamated Wood Turners, Tin-plate Workers,
Brass-founders, Boltmakers, Plumbers, Card
Strippers and Grinders, Amalgamated Iron-
founders (two branches), Cloggers, and Machine
Grinders.

The procession was headed by the General
Committee, wearing red, white, and blue rosettes;
and most of the societies had with them bands of
music and banners. Badges were worn by the
processionists to distinguish the respective so-
cieties to which they belonged. The operative
spinners wore cotton buds. The fustian cutters
displayed a model cutting frame and banner. The
amalgamated engineers wore white rosettes and
streamers, and the superannuated members of
their society followed in carriages. The brick-
layers, too, provided a carriage for their
aged members. The tin-plate workers had
tin stars and streamers ; brass medals dis-
tinguished the brass-founders; and the Amalga-
mated Iron founiers, whose superannuated members
were in a waggonette, lioro white rosettes and
streamers. The members of the respective socie-
ties were requested to meet in Union-street at
half-past two o'clock, and march thence to Spin-
ners' Gardens for the purpose of holding an out-
door meeting. The marshalling of the procession
occupied a longer time than wa.i expected, and it
was nearly half-past five before the first part of
the procession reachcd the ground, which is not
more than ten minutes' walk from the town. The
processionists were then glad to obtain a relief
from the strict order of the programme, and not
more than one third remained to take part in
the meeting, at which several resolutions were pro-
posed.

The absence of Mr. George Potter, of London,
and Mr. I. Burnett, of Newcastle, who bad been
announced to speak, was no doubt a disappoint-
ment to many who were anxious to bear them.
The procession, walking three or four abreast, was
thirty-five minutes in passing a given point, and
tho conductors estimated that 8,000 or 10,000
were present.'

Addresses were delivered from two platforms or.
waggons; Mr. W. Harrison, hatter, presiding at
one, and Mr. F. Richardson, of the Amalgamated
Engineers; at the other. A letter was read ftom
Mr. G. Potter apologising for his inability to
attend the meeting, and stating that the Criminal
Law Amendment Act should have his entire
opposition until it had been modified or repealed.
The following is the substance of the proceed-
ings at No. 1 platform :
After a brief address by the Chairman, Mr. J.
B. Tattersall, operative cotton spinner, proposed—
" That this meeting is of opinion that the Criminal
Law Amendment Act is unjust and exceptional in
its character, invidious and oppressive in its prac-
tical application, as being specially directed against
trade unionists, who are pre-judged by its provi-
sions of harbouring criminal intentions; and here-
by pledges itself to use every legal and constitu-
tional means to obtain a speedy repeal of the said
Act, as being a piece of unjustifiable legislation
directed against the working classes of this
country."—The resolution, baying been seconded
by Mr. D. Hep Worth, joiner, and supported by
Mr. P. Shorrocks, Manchester, was passed.
On the motion of Mr. H. Hardy, seconded by
Mr. T. Blazedale; a petition embodying the above
resolution was adopted, with the request that the
members for Oldhau would present it to Parlia-
ment and support its prayer.
Mr. T. Ashton, secretary of the Oldham Opera-
tive Cotton Spinners' Association, moved—" Owing
to the rapid,, extension of the cotton trade since the
year 18,50, during which period the production has
increased over 90 per cent, and notwithetanding
the aid of improved machinery, 40 per cent. Ada,
tional labour has been entailed upon the factory
workers ; therefore, it is the opinion of this meet-
ing that the time has arrived when, having a due
regard to the health of women, young persons, and
children employed in factories, the hours of labour

should be reduced by legieleigse enactment from
60 to 64 per week." ,

Mr. J. Riley, president of the Association,
seconded, and Mr. Crossley, of Blackburn, supported
the resolution, which was passed.
On the motion of Mr. J. Ashton, Oldham,
seconded
,by Mr. W. Goddard, Oldham, the follow-
ing resolution was passed :--" That it is the con-
viction of this meeting that steps should at once be
taken to secure the passing of an Act of Parliament
reducing the term of factory labour from 60 to 54
hours per week; and that a petition embodying
the reasons why such an Act of
_Parliament has
become necessary be adopted, and the same to be
signed by the Chairman and forwarded to the
borough members for presentation to Parliament."
A resolution was also passed pledging those who
took part in the meeting to render all the support
they possibly could to those memhers of Parlia-
ment who were endeavouring to secure a limitation
of the hours of labour in factories for women,
children, and young persons.
Similar resolutions were passed at the other
platform, at which Mr. Daniel Quile made a
vigorous speech against the Act which was re-
ceived with great applause, and votes of thanks
were accorded to the chairmen.

articles.title: SCOTCH MASONS.
articles.text:
THE SCOTCH MASONS.

Our readers will have observed that a movement
by the most important trades in Greenock has
lately been set on foot, to consider the best means
whereby the above Act may either be wholly re-
pealed or amended, so as to be acceptable to the
working classes, against whom it presses with
extreme severity, in cases of trade disputes.
With a view of obtaining the opinions of the
Right Hon. H. A. Bruce, in his capacity as
Member for Renfrowshire, and Mr. Grieve,
Member for the town, Mr. Matthew Allan, secre-
tary to the eighteen trades represented by the dale
gates, at a meeting held on 22nd March, was
instnpted to communicate with those gentlemen,
which he did; and at a meeting held on Monday
night, in the Masons' Hall, Greenock, ho read the
folloising correspondence :
[Fnost Ma. %woe.]
' April 3, 1872.

firn,—l beg to acknowledge the receipt of your
letter of the 30th March, informing me that meet-
ngs of various trades had been held in Greenock
to consider the operation of the Criminal Law
Amendment Act, 1871, and requesting me, as
Representative of the County of Renfrew, to
inform you to what extent you may rfly upon my
assistance in obtaining the repeal of portions of
that Act which you object to as oppressive, and are
so framed as to subject workmen to punishments
for acts in themselves inoffensive.

I have recently been furnished by a deputation
of the Parliamentary Committee of the Trades
Union Congress with reports of the decisions of
cases under the Act. The time since the passing
of the Act has been one of unusual excitement in
the labour market. Numerous strikes, conducted
with much determination on both sides, have
occurred among some of the most important
trades. Groat numbers of workmen have conse-
quently been thrown out of employment. It is
therefore very satisfactory and highly creditable
to the working population throughout the Empire
to find that it has been found necessary to invoke
the aid of the law on comparatively few occasions.
The cases adjudicated under the Act which have
been supplied to me are twenty-two in number,
some of them, however, including more than one
defendant. Of these eases, seven were dismissed;
several others were of a slight character, punished
sometimes slightly, sometimes with a severity which
seems to me excessive. In a few instances con-
victions have taken place :which, judging from the
reports, do not seem to me to have been justified
by the Act. One conviction was reversed on
appeal; another is now under appeal. In several
icases the convictions appear to me just, and the
punishments not more than adequate to the
offence.

You state in your letter that under the third
clause pieketting is wholly illegil, however peace-
ably conducted, and that "the unionist is wholly
at the mercy of the supplanter." That this
statement is inaccurate is proven by the fact that
several eases of pickotting, not amounting to
coercion as defined by the Act, have been dis-
missed.

But I am bound to admit that in a few case
the Act has :been strained so as to include as
offences acts certainly not intended to be so re-
garded by the promoters of the Act, nor, I believe,
by re'rliament.
I shall be prepared to support any amendment
of the Act which shall remove ambiguities of ex-
pression leading to conflicting constructions, or
which tend to restore the Act to the form in which
it was promotei by Government.

But I am not prepared to recede from the princi-
ples on which the Act was framed, or to admit
.
that the offences which it was intended to repress
should be lefc to the ordinary liw of the land, ex
-
elusive of this statute. I think that the acts of

intimidation and molestation contemplated by the
measure as proposed by the Government were
proper subjects for legislation and for punishment.
I think that, while picketting in particular may be
conducted peaceably and inoffensively, it may also
be so entorced as to demand the interference of
the law; and while I would give the freest scope
to argument and peaceable persuasion in the con•
-
duet of trade disputes, I would protect workmen
from undue coercion, either by threats of the
character defined by the Ad, or by deeds of moles-
tation amounting to serious annoyance and obstruc-
tion.
I do not, however, think that Parliament will
be disposed to entertain any proposal for the
modification of the ACL until it bai had a greater
experience than it now possesses of its working.
A few legal decisions by Court of Authority
will clear away doubts and promote uniformity of
decision. After such experience it may be possible
to arrive at satisfactory conclusions as to the
alleged ambiguities and oppressive operation of
some of the provisions complained of.
It will be for you and your friends to decide
what course you will, under these circumstances,
pursue. I venture to dissuade immediate action
as premature and useless; but if it be taken, I
shall be ready to assist you within the limits I
have indicated.
I have the honour to be, SZr,
Your obedient servant,
11. A. BRUCE.

[From Mn. Gamut.]
House of Commons, 4th April, 1872.

Sir,---Thaving been in Scotland for a few days
during the Easter recess, I found your favour of
30th ult. on my return.
I have already expressed at the meeting with
my constituents last December, that several of the
provisions of the "Criminal Law Amendment Act's
are too strinient. Amendments Were introduced
in the Lords, on the Bill of last year, in the direc-
tion you refer to, but from the temper of the House
of Commons when the Bill came back, those who
had taken an active share in the management of
the" Trades' Union Bill" did not consider it prudent
to divide. I will see those gentlemen, and if any
action is to be taken this session, I shall be glad to
co-operate with them in reasonable amendments
on the "Criminal Law Amendment Act."
"I am, Sir, your obedient servant,

JAS. J. GRIBVE.

In the discussion which followed, Mr. Grieve's
letter was generally accepted as satisfactory; but
very strong exception was taken to the latter part
of Mr. Bruce's, where he admits the Act has been
strained, and unwarranted convictions had taken
place; yet, in face of this admission, he counsels
no action to be taken, virtually meaning that
enough of innocent, respectable trade unionist'
have not been sacrificed to an unjust and oppres-
sive law. It was argued, and we think with force,
that this reasoning of Mr. Bruce's is extremely
puerile, and shows a strong undercurrent of opinion
against trade unions.

A sub-committee was appointed to consider the
present Act, and that originally introduced by
Government, and to report to a future meeting
what they considered would he a proper definition
of the word "coercion," or what they consider
should form criminal actions during trade disputes.
