war with their masters. Strike has succeeded
Strike, and agitation been rife in every quar-
ter. There is scarcely one manufacturing
town which has not felt the effects of the con-
vulsion. To carry through this powerful
movement the most extensive combinations ,
were formed among the workmen. In some
instances all the tradesmen of a place bound
themselves to support one particular trade
while on Strike; in others the members of one
trade in different places formed a league to
enable their friends in one locality to commence
the attack. Such was the strength gained by
this web of blended alliances, that strikes
were prolonged for months, and negotiations
carried on with the most eminent masters, not
as with superiors, but as with equals, who had
quite as much to lose as their adversaries, or
even more. Throughout the tone of the work-
men was quiet, though resolute and uncom-
promising, and as the movement was by far
the most comprehensive of the kind over wit-
nessed in Germany so it was the most enemas-

tug.
The Strikes were directed by improvised
committees, whose members mostly belonged to
one of the various Socialistic societies. These
societies themselves are not particularly
favoured by the workmen of this country, and
at the highest estimate count only from
150,000 to 200,000 devotees. As they, more-
over, are divided into three parties, each
intent upon realising the socialistic ideal in
their own way, and anything but on friendly
terms with the others, it had been hoped that
their influence upon the mass of the working
classes would not be very material for some
time to come. The Strikes of 1871 have
destroyed this fond illusion. Whether the
German Socialists, under the orders of Lieb-
knecht and Bebel, rally round the Inter-
national, and regard a Itepulilic as the neces-
sary preliminary to Communism; whether,
with Herr Mende, they call upon the Govern-
ment to confiscate all capital and become the
only employer, or whether, following the lead
of the versatile Herr von Schweitzer, they offer
to befriend the authorities if permitted to
coerce the middle classes in a.hundred minor
particulars, Knee absolute confiscation is
impossible,—all these divisions have been
Unanimous in supporting the Strikes of the
working classes, and, as a rule, have suc-
ceeded in conducting them according to their
own special views. To effect this did not give
them much trouble; they only required to
depute a small number of their men to the
meetings of the malcontents, with orders to
harangue them in the usual
.pliraseoingy of
their class. By long theoretical
.occupation
with the subject, by superior intelligence,. and
the enthusiastic ardour of their convictions,
these deputies managed to usurp the direction
of hundreds of thousands, who were either
ignorant of the ulterior purposes of the sect or
else directly opposed to them.
Ia their origin the strikes were not unjusti-
fiable. Even upon the assumption that the
former rate of wages was satisfactory, the
workmen had a right to demand an increase.
Seeing that rent and provisions had become so
much dearer, why should not manual labour
too
.1) It is admitted on all hands that the cost
of living at Berlin has been doubled for large
strata of the middle classes in the last six or
seven years, and increased 60 or 70 per cent.
even for the poor. It is nearly, though not

quite, the same thing in other 'considerable
towns. Who, then, can blame the workmen
for advancing a claim that their pay, which
was certainly never excessive, should at least
keep pace with what was exacted for house-
rent and eatables? More especially, who can
be severe upon their demand at a time when
the middle classes are making money so fast,
and when the growing riches of their betters
have so much contributed to render the necea.
saries of life dearer for the proletariat?
The Strikes began by the working men asking
for an increase of wages 25 per cent., and a
reduction of hours from 12 to 10. When they
obtained their terms peace was re-ostablished ;
when they had to give in the attack was re-
sumed a little later, and, in many cases, with
better success. The result of the entire
campaign is a general rise of the price of labour
by 25 per cent. in a single year—a figure the
more remarkable because a like increase had
been gradually effected in the six preceding
years. A few, but not very many, trades have
been likewise victorious in the question of
hours; and highly skilled labourers, I am
told, may almost count upon twice the
remuneration they received shortly before

the war.
A few details will serve to illustrate these
general remarks. The Strike of the Berlin
masons began in the June of last year, and
went on for six weeks. The workmen de-
manded an increase of their daily wages from
2s. 3d. to 35., a reduction of hours from 12 to
10, and extra pay of sd. for each hour over-
time. Upon this the 300 builders of Berlin
formed a counter association, which negatived
the programme of the Working men in tutu.
Negotiations were repeatedly resumed, but as
often broken off, both parties remaining firm.
At last the masters gave in upon the condition
that their defeat should be concealed under
some concessions of a merely formal nature.
Since then the workmen have been giving
their services for something like eleven hours
at 3s. 6d. per day. While the Strike lasted
about a thousand workmen left Berlin;
another 5,000 quietly remained here, being
supported by the voluntary contributions of
the other trades, which were ample enough
for each man to receive ss. per week. The
rest of their wants was provided for by the
men finding chance work or making their
wives and daughters ply the needle and scrub
the floor more diligently than ever. If
the worst came to the worst, a visit was
paid to the pawnbroker. The total
expenditure of the Strike Committee was
computed at £B,OOO, a residue of £lOO
being left in their coffers on the resumption of
work. An even vaster operation was the
joiners' Strike, which broke out after that of
the masons had been settled, and lasted nine
weeks. Of the 8,000 joiners in the city, 6,000
struck; 2,000 went oft elsewhere; while 1,000,
married people with large families, remained
staunch to their work. The claims put forth
were similar to those of the masons-25 per
cent. more wages, and a reduction of time to
91 hours. The masters, who in Berlin num-
ber no less than a thousand, with 300 wealthy
contractors among them, answered these de-
mands by the counter-proposition that piece
work, which had not been very general, should
be made universal, after which they hoped to
be able to allow higher wages. To this
the joiners retorted that as they required an
inalienable guarantee for higher wages in the
ease of piece work, they must insist upon an
increase of daily wages being conceded. This
reply put a stop to negotiations, the working
men's committee deolininc, to entertain the
compromise proposed by the masters. During
the nine following weeks 'every married man
received Gs. and every bachelor 4s. 6d.
per week from the strike funds. After the
expiration of seven weeks those masters
who had taken coutraot work for builders,
and who, owing to the steady increase of house-
rent, were enabled to accord higher wages,
began to relent. Thus an opening was made
for a compromise, by which the weekly wages
formerly at from 15s. to 21s. were raised to
from 21s. to 255., the number of hours remain-
ing the same. Piece work under the new con-
ditions yields from 30s. to 365. per week.
Similar trials of strength were resorted to by
the other trades and have also ended in victory
for the men. Tho example set by Berlin and
the larger manufacturing towns generally was
not lost upon the smaller places, which were
obliged to raise their prices without the actual
compulsion of a Strike. The miners likewise
reaped some of the fruits of the campaign.

The agricultural labourers have rooted by
the general rise least of all. - Thefr pay Varies
greatly in the different parts of 'the country,
and cannot easily be caloulated a Money, kg
it mostly consists of substantial advantages in
the way of food, clothing, house rent, and the
free use of laud, &e. Generally speaking,
however, the agricultural labourer receives
from a fourth to a third less than the worst
paid mechanic, and the difference is probably
even greater than it was now that the wages
in the towns have risen in a"feii years 30 per

added in the country. But the field hand in'
Germany has a more exalted object in life than
high wages. His ideal is emigration.. Owing

SATURDAY, APRIL 20, 1872.

THE FIRST BLOW AT THE HOUSE OF

LORDS.

THE Resolution introduced by the Loup
CHANCELLOR to abolish the appellate jurisdic-
tion of the House of Lords, and to reconstruct
upon a new basis the Courts of final appeal,
is one of groat interest. It declares, "That
it is expedient that one Imperial Supreme
Court of Appeal be established which shall sit
continuously for the hearing of all matters
now heard by way of appeal before this House
or before the Judicial Committee of the Privy
Council; and that the appellate jurisdiction of
this House be transferred to such Supreme
Court of Appeal." This project stands over
for individual consideration before discussion
and disposal. In the meantime, to all eon-
stitutional politicians, whether lawyers or
laymen, the main proposal must be very
striking. "Ono of the oldest of our judicial
institutions," as one daily contemporary has
remarked, "one of the most showy an

imposing of the curious anomalies of our
constitutional system, was threatened with
complete abolition and extinction, and the
House of Lords and, its galleries showed no
greater interest than if a Turnpike Bill had
been the business of the sitting." Let us
follow Lord HATIIERLEY in the exposition
of this remarkable feature of the mea-
sure. In point of fact, he said, their
Lordships' appellate jurisdiction had never
been exercised without considerable con-
test, and, about a quarter of a century ago,
had, in the case of Mr. O'CoNNELL, been
virtually abandoned. Since then, it had been
an obvious fiction to speak of decisions really
arrived at by a small Committee of their Lord-
ships, as decisions of the House of Lords.
Indeed, long before that, "the House of •

Lords" had only meant the LORD CHANCELLOR,
with or without another lawyer, aid one or
two lay lords to make a quorum. In order to
obtain the assistance of those lay peers, it
had been once recommended that there should
be a ballot to determine who should sit with
the LORD CHANCELLOR, and that there should
be a fine for non-attendance. In Lord LYND-
HURST'S time Lord HATHER.LEY, though not
then at the bar, remembered the shame with
which he had to explain to an eminent
French jurisconsult, whom he accompanied to
the House, that, when an appeal lasted more
days than one, the lay lords were different at
each sitting. The shorter tenure of office
now-a-days enjoyed by Lord Chancellors had
increased the number of law lords. In 1856,
however, a Select Committee reported against
the system, and pointed out the grievances
arising from the irregular attendance of the
law lords, the limited number of their sittings,
the consequent delay and expense entailed by
such a tribunal. In the face of facts like
these, attempts were made to pooh-pooh a plain
working man when, at the conference called in
Birmingham, concerning the hereditary cha-
racter of the House of Lords, he referred to
the judicial functions exercised in its name as
an additional reason for looking closely into its
constitution, and considering whether, if not
wholly abolished, it should not be thoroughly
reformed. The facts which, as then moderately
stated, were boldly disputed, are now more
largely repeated on the high authority of the
actual LOUD CHANCELLOR, and will find, we

articles.title: IRONFOUNDERS' SOCIETY.
articles.text:
THE IRONFOUNDERS' SOCIETY.

THE Committee of the Ironfounders' Society
have laid before their members their sixty-
second yearly report. It shows an improve-
ment even to that of the preceding year. The
succeeding twelvemonths have been a period of
continuous prosperity. Both in money and in
numbers the society is no' better off than for
some years before. The members, also, are in an
improved position. They get higher wages,
and they work shorter hours. They have had
neither disputes nor strikes. The obnoxious
Criminal Law Amendment Act has not touched
them in person, though it touches them in feel-
ing, as a threatening, oneesided statute, of
which it is their duty to their brother working
men to demand the repeal. "We feel con-
fident," is the language of the report, "that
nothing but the demand for labour in our
department of trade has kept us safe from the
olutehea of this bad law."

The contributions of the year are .C 28,134.
In 1870, although in seven months out of the
twelve the individual paymentyas 2s. a week,
the income was not more than £29,597. The
difference, which is but £1,463 will seem still
less, when it is borne in mind, that, for three
months in the year just expired, the society
has been worked at a still further reduotion
of the weekly payment. The lesson which
this teaches is, the wisdom of keep-
ing as close as possible to the one shilling
a week. Nevertheless, it is claimed for
the Ironfounders that no trade is ;more ready
than they are to make sacrifices for the leas

fortunate among their brethren. The popu-
larity of the society with the trade is shown'
by the amount of entrance money, which has
jumped up from £756 in 1870 to £1,586 in
1871, more than double in one twelvemonth.
In short, as to the receipt side of the amount,
after paying accident claims and expenses to
£2,482, and loans and interest to £489, the
increase of cash in hand upon the year stands
at the high figure of £12,250.
The showing afforded by the expenditure
side of the sheet is equally, if not more en-
couraging. First, as to out-of-work relief;
in 1867, this cost the society £35,272 ; in 1871,
£5,447 ; or less than a sixth of the former
sum, being, in fact, the smallest amount
in any one year since 1860. The amount
'paid for sickness has been somewhat in excess
over the foregoing year, but that for funerals
considerably less. The superannuation expen-
diture remains pretty stationary. In accidents,
the Society has been able to clear off " a lot
of arrears" which had accumulated during
depression in trade, paying the large sum of
£2,482 in a single year. This is a noble testi-
mony to the " friendly " character of such
societies; but one other fact remains to be
mentioned, which, we dare say, even those
who hold the "International" in most dread
and abhorrence, will admit to be a fair illus-
tration of the Divine saying, "It is more
blessed to give than to receive." To the
Moulders of Chicago, while suffering from the
burning of that city, the handsome donation
of fifty pounds was sent from the Friendly
Society of Ironfounders of England, Ireland,
and Wales.

articles.title: INTERNATIONALISM AND BAILIE COCHRANE.
articles.text:
INTERNATIONALISM AND BAILIE
COCHRANE.

BAILIE COCHRANE, Member for the Isle o
Wight, is a staunch Conservative, lo which
we do not object; he is also an excite& alarmist
of the most doleful type, and to this we object
very strongly. Like all men of this sort, he
overacts his part when he sets about getting
up a cry. To overdo is to undo; and Mr.
BAILIE COCHRANE is clever at this sort of
active futility. People with clear practical
ideas, if they desired to believe him, could
not do so. His melodrama has in it too much
of the dagger, the mask, and the poison
bowl. He does not invent falsehoods, being,
no doubt, too much of a gentleman for that;
but he submits himself to be crammed by
parties who, to say the least, have not a
very high respect for accurraey of state-
ment. He told the House of Commons
that there were 180,000 enrolled members of
the International Society in England, who
were totally ignorant of its real objects when
they joined it, but who, no doubt, by this time
have gained possession of its character, aims,
and policy; men who are at the present
moment prepared to vindicate its principles
and carry out its plans. What these prin-
ciples and plans are we shall state in Mr.
BAILIE COCHRANE'S own words, which are
too definite and precise to alter without injury
to their significance, and we desire that their
full mewling should be understood. These
principles strike at the "root of all morality,
all civilisation, all rights of property, and all
belief in God."
Pretty stiffish this, as a description of what
180,000 organised men in England believe in
and aim at, and a most dangerous and signifi-
cant fact, if it be not what is far more likely,
a most absurd and ridiculous fancy. It
would be simply an insult to the
understandings of English working men
to defend them from the foolish
charges of Mr. COCHRANE. Can any living
man soberly state that 180,000 men of any
class in England could be drawn into such a
society as that described without knowing
what meaning there was in it, or that having
discovered its meaning to be what our alarmist
describes, would remain one moment in it
after making that discovery? When Mr.
COCHRANE, Mr. EASTIVICK, and others speak
of a hogs organisation called an International
Society, they should define its meaning. Mr.
COCHRA.NR is the only one in the House who
has attempted this, and his description is
simply ludicrous. Mr. Fiwcirres attempt
was more inclusive, but not much more
aoourato, as he brought in Messrs. LOWE and

DisnAEu as advocates of International, or

Socialist ideas. It is pretty clear, however,
that on the subject of Socialism, Mr. FAWCETT
himself needs information. That there is a
society called. the International we know;
what its numbers are we do not
know. That certain parties on its behalf
have written and spoken most pernicious trash
is just as certain as that certain other parties
have written and spoken mendacious nonsense
against it. What we are certain of is this—
that if either Mr. COCHRANE'S or Mr. Ekw-
CETT'S description of the International be true,
it has not, and never can have, any large
number of members amongst the working men
of England. The general body of our Trades
Unionists know what they are about as well as
the gentlemen of the House of Commons, and
they certainly are not dreaming of promoting
such insane nonsense as that referred to in the
debate on Mr. COCHRANE'S question. The co-
operators of England are engaged in a very
practical work, which is as directly opposed
to the wild schemes described as light is to
darkness.

The sort of wretched outcry now sought to be
raised has always been common enough at
certain intervals. Some of the best men the
world ever saw have been thus accused;
and these men, whatever their character,
have been charged with desiring to uproot all
morality, to attack all property, and to destroy
religion by a blank denial of the existence of
GOD. Poor blatant BAILIE COCHRANE simply
repeated a string of old accusations, always
resorted to by knaves and fools when trouble-
some persons or novel principles had to be
attacked. That there are some hundreds, or
even thousands, of Internationalists few will
doubt; but of such as BAILIE Cocna.usE
described; it is not credible that there are two
dozen in all broad England. That they have
violent, empty-headed men amongst them need
not be disputed. But to suppose that English
property, or order, or religion is endangered
by the handful of men who meet in London to
address each other as " citizen " SAIITII or
" citizen " BROWN, is simply absurd. England
has her fair average of fools, who in times of
excitement become active; some of them describe
themselves as operative Conservatives, and
some as Internationalists. And some aro to
be found in the House of Commons spouting
alarmist nonsense when they ought to be
turning their attention to something with a
little practical good sense in it. If, instead
of frightening themselves by exaggerating the
importance of Internationalism, our legislators
could meet and overcome the danger at present
manifesting itself in our agricultural districts,
not because the people have false ideas, but
because they have unendurable wants and no
ideas whatever, a much better result would
be obtained from their labours than can ever
be obtained from any amount of nonsensical
talk they may indulge in about the balderdash
of English revolutionists whose bark is far
more alarming than their bite, and who will
become quiet and harmless enough if left to
themselves.

LABOURERS' STRIKE.
AT this period of the agitation we do no

wish to direct the attention of the publics from
the main question at issue between the farmers
and their labourers. The labourer is demand-
ing more wages, and it is desirable that he
should attend to that demand, and nothing
else until it is obtained.
There are several points necessary to be
looked to for this purpose. Those who con-
sider what is asked for reasonable and right
should subscribe whatever they can spare—
pence or pounds— to help them. Those who
can procure situations for men on strike should
procure them, and draft the idle men to where
their labour can be more profitably employed.
Friends and agents of emigration ought to put
their shoulders to the wheel that the danger-
ous pressure in the districts on strike may be
removed. Every practical step should be
taken to make the efforts of the poor suffering
labourers successful. And above all men, the
Trades Unionists of the great manufacturing
towns ought to lend a helping hand. Their
employment was never more brisk, or their
funds never so abundant as they are now. A
generous tote of money from the great Unions

would put hope, life, power into this move-

ment ; and if the necessary sympathy and the
requisite good sense to prompt this should exist
anywhere, in any class, it should be found
amongst the men who know so well what the

unhappy farm labourer has to suffer in his
poor home whilst endeavouring to bring up his
children honestly on twelve shillings a week.

Let this battle be won for the labourer aud
by the labourer, and a new day will dawn in
England for the humbler classes. We are told
the farmer cannot afford to pay. This, how-

ever, is not the labourer's look out. Labour is
his commodity, and he has a perfect right to
get the highest price for it he can. In doing
this he is but following the example set him by
every other class of the community. The
butcher does not lower the price of his meat
because the labourer cannot afford to pay for
it. Justice is not cheapened because, as a
marketable commodity in the hands of the
lawyers, it is beyond the poor man's
reach. Land is charged for up to what
it will bring, whether to cultivate or
build on, whatever the means may be of

those who require it. What would anybody
think of a class of persons, whether they called
themselves political economists or philan-
thropists, who went about the world preaching
up the duty of studying other men's require-
ments rather than our own. It is true that
this doctrine, or something like it, was preached
in an out-of-the-way corner of the world nearly
nineteen hundred years ago; but it has long
been exploded, and driven out from amongst
men, except as a pleasant impossibility to
talk about. The Church regards it as unortho -
dox, and the Dissenters have not made it the
ground of any one of their many separations
from the Church.

We are told that much of the land. at presen
in cultivation will not pay if the labourers in-
sist on receiving fifteen shillings a week. We
reply, let it go out of cultivation; that's the
landlord's look out. Possibly too, poor farmers
may have to give up their holdings if the
labourers insist on their present demands. So
be it. This is a question for landlords and far-
mers. If the labourer can only live in the
country by remaining in the brute's condition
in which we find him, itis time he cleared out,
and went where his life may become more in-
dependent and manly.
Mr. DISRAELI and others would fain persuade
the public that the labourers' condition has
improved with the general improvement of
the country. It would not be right to accuse
a gentleman of his standing and experience of
ignorance. If he is not ignorant, however,
he is something very much worse. His state-
ment, if true, is quite capable of proof, and
facile as he is with tongue and pen, we defy
him to prove it. The question is not whether
the agricultural labourer has advanced in
proportion to the advance of other classes.
We shall not put such an impossible task on'
Mr. DISRAELI ; we simply ask him to prove
any advance at all. Men now can read history,
and those who have examined know something
of the condition of the field-worker at the
time when the HENRYS and EDWARDS bore
sway in the land. We know something
of it now also, or Parliamentary Commissions
are very silly and very expensive farces.
It is not very long since HUGH Sumorn
TREMENILEERE and EDWARD CARLTON TUF-
NELL signed one of these reports, which was
presented to Parliament, and which Mr. Ohs-
BLEU ought to have read, if he has not. If so,
it would be curious to find out if this little
rural sketch crossed his mind when speaking
of the " rosy-cheeked" children of the
labourer. It was drawn by Mrs. ANTrioNY
kraals, labourer's wife, of Denton, Hunting-
donshire. It is to be found at page 12 of that
report—" In June, 1862, my daughters,
HARRIET and. SARAII, aged respectively 11 and
13 years, were engaged by a ganger ' to
work on Mr. MORIUN'S land at Stilton. They
worked there six.weeks, going and returning
each day—the distance going and coming was
sixteen miles—besides which they worked
in the fields from eight in the morning to five
or half-past five in the afternoon. They had
7d. a day, and had to find their own meals, as
well as their tools (hoes). The 'ganger' per-
suaded me to send my little girl &aux, who
was then six years of age; she walked all the

way (8 miles) to Peterborough to her work,
and worked from eight to half-past five, and
received4d. She was that tired that her sisters
had to carry her the best part of the way home-
-8 miles—and she was ill from it for three
weeks, and never went again." We do not
say that these children had not "rosy cheeks."
There are blessings ,and beauties given by
Heaven which the worst wickedness of men
cannot utterly obliterate. But notwithst and-
the children's "roses," can Englishmen tole-
rate a system of treatment towards the poor
which permits, as even an occasional thing,
such abominations as this?

Whatever is necessary to alter such a con-
dition of things must be adopted. lf lower
rent is necessary, then we must have lower
rent. If his estate at lower rental will not
pay the landlord, let him sell out and take
what it will bring, and emigrate. We can
spare him better than we can the honest,
willing, worker. Other men besides landlords
make bad bargains occasionally. If he is in-
disposed to do this, then let him and the
farmer quietly settle their conditions of
tenancy with each other,and treat the labourer,
so as to make the condition of the man whose
face they have been so long grinding, some-
thing not utterly unendurable, something
not absolutely disgraceful to our character as a
Christian and civilised people.

articles.text:
THE AMERICAN CLAIMS.

THE last repot t from the other sid is, that the
Washington Government had decided 'to with-
draw the claims for indirect damages. There
were not wanting other evidences of a growing
opinion among the most intelligent and
moderate men in the States against any such
demands. One of the highest, if not the
highest, authority in matters of international
law bad pronounced against them in that New
York journal (The Independent), which is re-
pteud to have the widest circulation. On the
clear ground that the terms of the Treaty do
not warrant them, PROFESSOR WOOLSEY con-
tended for their withdrawal. This gentleman
is well-known to have watched the whole
matter closely from the beginning. He
answered Mr. SUMNER'S first speech on the
subject by an article in the North American
Review. Until recently, ho was President of
Yale College, perhaps the highest place of
learning in the States. Anything from the
pen of such a man is believed to have the right
of authority in the minds of his fellow
citizens.

Meanwhile, the Counter Case of the British'
Government has been put in. At the first
sitting of the Geneva Tribunal, no arbitrator
was present. They will not meet till the
middle of June. The correspondence on the
subject shows that nothing had yet occurred
to prejudice the position of either party before
the tribunal. The British Case discusses the
American claims, and declares them to be
so loose and unsatisfactory, and so plainly
excessive in amount, that they cannot be
accepted, even as furnishing a prima facie basis
of calculation." The consequences to neutral
Powers, were the views set up to be sanctioned,
are considered as very serious. For the first
time in history,the British Government believes,
it has been urged, that every act or omission,
however insignificant, on the part of a neutral
Government, is to be made foundation for
pecuniary demands. Were this principal
adopted, the only prudent course would be to
decline all intercourse with belligerents, or,
especially in the case of smaller States, to seek
alliance with one of the Powers at war. The
British Government is convinced that the
Arbitrators will not sanction these extreme
views, which even the States themselves would
never accept as binding in practice.

THE WAGES BILL.

TgE Select Committee appointed by the
House of Commons to consider the Wages
Bill, brought in by Mr. WifiTEnno.rfp4, as
Under-Secretary for the Home Department,
met for the first time on Monday morning, Mr.
GATHORNE Hum in the chair. Having de-
cided that no evidence 'should be taken at the
first sitting, they proceeded to discuss the
provisions of the Bill with closed doors, and,
on rising, adjourned to Monday next. It may
be well, in the meantime, to recapitulate the
principal parts of the measure. It provides
that wages shall be payable in coin of the
realm, without any deduction, and without
any condition as to the spending of any part
thereof; and that every, master and master's
agent who makes any contract, deduction, or
payment declared illegal, shall be guilty of an
offence against the Act. Under the old -Act,
certain deduations were allowed to be made by
employers for goods supplied to workmen.
The present Bill proposes to abolish the right
of making such deductions in the shape .of a
set-off; and one of the points upon which the
Committee will have to decide is, whether
the master shall have the right to sue for
materials supplied by him. By the sixth
clause provision is made for the weekly pay-
ment of• wages, or:at such intervals less than
a week as may be specially arranged. This is
a new prevision. Neither the Present Bill nor
the existing Act applies to Ireland, but, several
Irish members having expressed a desire that
it should do so, the ATTORNEIC-DENERAL for
IRETAND intends making provision for that pur
pose.

CULTURAL DISTRICTS.

7'irE Methodist I,4ecorder, the more Liberal of
the two Wesleyan newspapers, takes notiee of
the fad that some local preachers are mixed
up in the Warwickshire and other agricultural
movements. "A fire," says our contemporary,
"has been kindled which it will be impossible
to quench by threats, by violence, by any
exercise of mere authority. Suddenly the farm
labourer, hitherto considered or:litany ignorant
and impassive, has awoke from the torpor of
ages to a consciousness of the inferiority of his
position and remuneration as compared with
that of the working hands in trade or manu-
facture; and it would be as imposaible to retard
the rising Of the ocean tide as to bring back
the condition of things, even only six months.
ago, previous to this awakening." Among
others who have narrowly watched th,e stir, is
Lord SIDNgY GpDOIRIIIN OSBORNE, a noble
clergyman of broad views who often writes in
the Times. The Reverend Lop, having given
special prominence to Methodism as one of the
principal springs of the movement, the Methodist
.Recorder accepts the imputation. "Although,"
says the Editor,' " he is in error in supposing,
that, as a class, the labourers meet sepa-
rate from all others in the smaller village
dispels—for the farmer who employs labour
is to be found there as well as the peasant who
is employed—still, it maybe acknowledged
that there is much of truth in the picture.
Unquestionably the labourer finds in connec-
tion with the public worship and schools and
classes connected with the chapel arecognition
I

of his manhood, and a degree of freedom which
he coii.ld never realise ia the parish church,
where the minister is associated in his mind
with the squire of the parish, and with a
system whose principal teaching practically
is that it is his duty as a poor man to stand at
a reverent distance and do homage
.to his
betters." The Times correspondent alluded
specially to the sympathy produced by the
ministrations of the local preachers in these
village chapels. He spoke of them as "minis-
ters," in ignorance of the special meaning
attached to that word by Methodists, as denot-
ing those set apart to the sacred office. Rarely,
if ever, do these Methodist preachers go aside
from religious teaching. They have not
hitherto in prayer or preaching dealt with
political or social matters. Churchman and
landowner although he is, he remarks, that, if
the new movement should continue under
such guidance, there is little fear of its leading
to any but a satisfactory issue. There will be
a powerful religioUs time given to it by its
real 'leaders being of the labouring
_Class.
"These are the men," he observes, "to whom
I look, if this contest is to be fought out, as
the chief instruments to procure moderation
in the claims of the labourers, submission to
the law in. their prosecution. They know—
none better—the history of every parish. They
have an influence capable of exercise in this
matter it were folly to deny. They have the
car of the labourer in his highest interests; to
them he will now listen in his struggle to
amend his earthly state."
The commentary of the Methodist Recorder
on the facts and admissions is brief, but it is
impressive:—" What an emphatic and re-
markable testimony to the influence of Metho-
dism in the agricultural districts! How is it,
that the Establishment, which his its hold
pre-eminently in the rural districts, has no
greater or more effectual hold upon the poor
of those districts? How is it, that, in a social
movement of this description, the working'
people find their natural and trusted guides,
not among the clergy, but among the preachers
of the Methodists, who, by the eon tossion
above quoted, are neither firebrands, nor
mountebanks, nor deceivers, but honest men
to whom those in power now look as to those
who can alone prevent the Spread Of hopeless
incendiarism and mischief?"

ANOTHER ANTI-PAPAL -INDICATION.
TUE KING of ITALY is stated to have made•
a large contribution in money towards the
erection of a Tational monument in commemo.
ration of SANONAMOLA.. This act is highly sig-
nificant. That eminent Italian, like LUTIIE a,
a monk, became, like LUTHER, a Reformer.
He flourished towards the close of the fifteenth
century. He was the SPURGEON of Florence.
Speaking like a prophet, he boldly rebuked
the tins of the day, and warned his hearers
of coming judgments. His predictions came
to pass. His tone was dernoctratic, and he
bearded the haughty Lonertzo, head of the
3/pipiot family, in his palace. The his-
torians are not agreed as to the precise
manner in which that celebrated aristocrat
took the plain :peaking of the intrepid monk.
It is certain, however, that, after the death of
the great Florentine: noble, SAVOICAROLL
became leader, of the party which claimed the
restoration of popular freedom, and led them
to victory. Of course, the oligarchical faction
took oars to charge them with heresy at Rome,
and, refusing to appear, he was excommuni-
cated. Such a diigrace was high honour,
especially at the hands of the wretch BORGIA..

SAVONAROLL had been for long an unsparing
denouncer of the corruption of the priests; he
now attacked their like-rninded head, the
POPE. He declared ALELINDER the SIXTII to
be a usurper, and promised, if the Princes
would convoke a general council, to prove his
illegitimacy as POPE and his false pretensions
to the name of Christian. In the end, how-
ever, his noble impulses transported him
beyond himself, and he passed from generom
enthusiasm into piteous fanaticism. The Porz
made arrantements-for putting him to torture.
Flinching at the prospect, he made humbling
admissions. These, however, did not serve
him. He was condemned to death, and first'
strangled, then burned. The cruel POPE
died; it is said through drinking by mifitsko

of some wine which he and his more cruel son
CESARE BORGIA, had poisoned in order to get
rid of an obnoxious Cardinal. Be this as it
may, SAVONAROLA, as a monk, was anti-papal,
and, as a native of Ferrara, an Italian patriot.
It is in these characters that the nation and
the KING propose doing lasting honours to his
memory.

THE PEOPLES GARDENS (WILLESDEN).
The opening of the above gardens and grounds
(pleasantly situated at Old Oak Common, near
Willesden Junction, and about fifty acres in
extent) for their third season is announced to take
place on Saturday, the 4th of May, under the
immediate personal superintendence of Mr. Henry
Boketer, of the German School, Foley-street,
Mary Mono. During the recess several important
improvements, both in the buildings and grounds,
affording increased comfort and accommodation "to
the visitors, have been carried out, and the rail-
way accommodation is largely• increased; trains
are continually coming to the Willesden junction
from all stations on the Metropolitan and District
lines, and also from the ,Euston and Broad-street
stations of the North Western lino. Those gar-
dens are in future to be conducted upon a novel
principle, to ensure the full carrying out of the
object with which they were established, not
as a commercial speculation, but as a healthy,
rational, and intellectual place of recreation, both
on week days and Sunday, for the working
classes and their families, free from those
contaminating surroundings too frequently
to be met with in the public gardens
in the hands of private speculators. The

tp members only, and all products that may be

tainments, lectures, fireworks, athletic sports, gym-
nastics, cricket, croquet, So., &c.; while on Sunday'

company's band and choir will attend, and give

Lectures will be delivered On scientific) and other

Evenings for the People" atSt. George's Hall,
The opening on the 4tli a bitty next will be

mond Beales, Esq., the Rev. Henry Solly, D.

BUILDING SOCIETY.
Oa Wednesday evening, at six o'clock, a pub

meeting was held at the London Bridge Rooms,
Wellington-stre3t, for the purpose of explaining
the objects and principles of the above society. The
Bishop of Winchester, who is the president of the
society, was announced to take the chair, and was
present at the above hour, but in eonsequence of a
rather private engagement was compelled to leave,
when the chair was taken by Colonel Beresford,
M.P., who spoke at some length on the useful-
ness of well-conducted building societies to the
working classes. Mr. W. Baxter then explained
the object of the society, which ,it was desired
should embrace as many bona fide working men as
possible, and for that purpose the shares had been
fixed at the small sum of £2 108. each, and the
minimum payment on each share only H. per
week. There were no fines for non-payment in
times of sickness or want of employment, and
many other advantages which could only be gua-
ranteed by a large number of members. The so-
ciety commenced operations on the 24th February
last, and up to the present date there has been
11,000 shares taken. The Bishop of Winchester
had consented to be president of the society, and
the vice-presidents were Sir IL Hoare, 3.1•1!” Mr.
H. Lewis, M.P., Mr- Torrens, M.P., Mr. Halms,
the Rev. John Mee, and Mr. IL Praed. The trus-
tees were Sir John Bennett, Mr. Baxter, and Mr.
Muggeridge ; and the arbitrators were Mr. S.
Locke, M.P., Col. Bere;iford; M.P., Morgan
Howard, Esq., E. Clarke, Esq., and the Rev:
Hugh Allen. All these gentlemen have been seen,
and approved of the rules. The directors were all
working men well-known in South London. He
concluded by moving a resolution approving of
the society and pledging the meeting to aid in
its extension. The Rev. Mr. Tarver seconded the
resolution, which was supported by Mr. Herbert
Praed and Mr. W. House, and AIL Thompeon,
working men, who paid thet the pooiety promised
to become one of the largest and most influential
buildingsocietiesin the kingdom. Several questions
having been asked from the body of the meeting,
as to the proposed working of the society, and theso
baying been satisfactorily answered, the resolution
was unanimously adopted. The Ray. Mr.
Wetherell, Mr. R. Keates, Mr. Ireland (working
men), and the Rev. Mr. Bowetead having addressed
the meeting, the proceedings concluded with a vote
of thanks to the chairman. At the close of the
meeting, which was attended by about 500 persons,
mostly working men, a considerable number of
shares were taken up.

articles.title: LITERATURE.
articles.text:
LITERATURE.

The People's Blue Book. By CIIA.RLES T EN-
NANT. Fourth Edition, revised, enlarged,
and brought down to the Present Tune; with
a Supplementary Chapter on Ireland. Crown
Svo. pp. 966, price 7s. 6d. sewed.
A new edition of this book has long been
called for, but the author has been very
reluctant to undertake the labour; the finan-
cial changes since the last edition' in 1862,
having so far altered the fades and figures as
, to require all the estimates and calculations
to be re-made, and a great part of the work
re-written, in order to bring it down to the
present time. It is now issued.
The object of the People's Blue Book is to
show that, in the author's opinion, the present
system of raising the revenue of the State is
unequal, unjust, extravagant, and in every
way injurious, because directly opposed to
sound principles, as laid down by Turgot,
i
Adam Smith, and Bastiat—that it s impos-
sible to amend a system so radically wrong;
the only remedy being in the simultaneous
abolition of all existing stamps and taxes
(except postage stamps, not properly a source
of revenue), and the substitution of an en-
tirely new system, founded on the only safe and
sound principle of equal justice to all classes.
The proposed new system is here set forth
with a minuteness of detail, which, in the
author's belief, presents the whole subject
with simple clearness to the commonest under-
standing; showing at the same time that, great
as wguld be the benefits to the working classes
in the cheapening of all the necessaries, com-
forts, and conveniences of civilised life, and
the general improvement of their social condi-
tion by enhancing the purchase-power of their
wages, etill greater would be the gain to the
middle and wealthier classes in the increased
value, more quiet enjoyment, and more secure
possession of their property.
The fiCope of the author's plan, much less its
details, cannot be adequately described within
the limits prescribed for this notice; but as the
proposed new system would be open to mis-
understanding on any imperfect and un-
detailed abstract of the plan, the book itself
may be referred to by those who desire to
consider its feasibility. The author has
less hesitation in making this suggestion,
from the fact that the price of the book is
less than the cost of printing .and paper. The
earnestness expressed in this unusual fact is
accounted for by his strong conviction that the
tendency of opinions in these times is to the
subversion of the rights of property and social
order, and ultimately the overthrow of the
English Monarchy and British Consfitution.
, The impression of impending danger has
prevailed over the author's reluctance to un-
dertake the laborious task of preparing a new
edition of this book for the people, in the firm
belief that the proposed scheme is the only
safe and effectual measure for averting the
threatened evils, by uniting the whole King-
dom on the sound. basis of equal justice to all
classes, thereby establishing free trade in
reality, and raising the prosperity of the United
Kingdom to an unexampled height. With the
same view the supplementary chapter on Ire-
land is addressed to the conscience and com-
mon sense of the Irish people.

articles.title: FEW WORDS TO THE WOUING CLASSES. –
articles.text:
A FEW WORDS TO THE WOUING
CLASSES. -

FELLOW WORKING -NEN,—I think at the pre-
sent time, now the supporters of Conservatism
are strenuously advocating their principles, as
those productive of more beneficial results to-
ward the welfare of our ()lass than those of
Liberalism, it behoves us, being so dependent
on the wisdom of the Legislature for our national
happiness, to think a little over the serious
responsibility of casting a vote, and before
committing our electoral influence either to
the one party or the other, to know what their
principles really consist of. Now, what does
Conservatism consist of? Well, I need not say
much to convince you that as far as we are
concerned as a class, it is impossible that we
can conscientiously give them our support,
because, in the first place, they do not recognise
the right of the franchise being extended to
working men untrammelled, and in a manner
that a man may vote, without the mercenary
question of pounds, shillings, and pence being
considered. They make it a question of how
much rent does the man pay, Secondly, they
do not recognise liberty of conscience in respect
to religion. They would force certain creeds
down our throats to use a vulgar term,
whether we dislike 4 them or otherwise. These
two reasons suffice in themselves (or ought to
do so) to prove to our minds that Conservatism
is not at all friendly to the interests of our
class. What does Liberalism consist of? Well,
true Liberalism (not the so-called Liberalism
prevailing in the House of Commons at the
present time) recognises just what its anta-
gonistic policy, Conservatism, does not—viz.,
the right of our class to have a voice in the
Government of our country, by giving us the
privilege of sending a representative to make
known our wants in the national gatherings
and councils of the State. Again, they. re-
cognize "Liberty of conscience," whereby men
may act as men, and not bathe mere tools of any

party that may happen to be in the ascendant
at the time being. So that we can readily see
that the Liberal policy is the one that we
working men should stand by. But the diffi-
culty is, how to discriminate 'twixt the true
and the false men that present themselves for
onr representatives in Parliament. One great
difficulty is, that instead of voting for a local
man, well known amongst us as a man of good
sound principle, we are apt to vote for an entire
stranger, whose only recommendation is that
he says he is a Liberal. If we would only
unite as a body, and select a gentleman whom
we could trust, not by his words, bat by hia
'actions, we should not find so-called Liberals
acting the part of a Conservative so well as
hardly to be able to tell the difference between
one and the other. Seeing that the probability
of a general eleution is imminent, we cannot do
better than act at once, and form into election-
eering committees, at once influential as a
Parliamentary body, instead of being, when
the time comes, paralysed, as it were, and
undecided whom to vote for or not.—Yours,
&c.,

GEORGE E. TYLEY.
2, The Terrace, London Road, Peckham, S.E

articles.title: OPENING OF THE BRITISH MUSEUM ON SUNDAYS.
articles.text:
THE OPENING OF THE BRITISH
MUSEUM ON SUNDAYS.

On Tuesday Mr. Harvey Lewis, M.P., and
Sir Charles Dilke, Bart., M.P., respectively
introduced to Lord Ripon deputations from
,hlio meetings held recently under the aus-
pices of the National Sunday League, in Mary -
lebone and Chelsea, for the purpose of promot-
ing the opening of the British Museum and
other national art galleries to the public on
Sundays. Mr. Slack, as chairman of the
Marylebone meeting, said it was constituted of
men emplayed in superior art work, who were
desirous of promoting their own education
and that of their order. They considered there
was nothing unreasonable in asking what
would be a great boon to a very large number
of persons at the expense of Sunday labour on
the part of a very few, and. he pointed out
that a large quantity of viork was done pow
by working men at their own homes generally
known as chamber work, because they had no
place provided for them of intellectual or
soientiflo resort. The gardens at Kew and
Hampton Court, since they had been thrown
open on the Sabbath had been largely patron-
ised by all classes of people, but they were
beyond the reach of many of the working
class. He showed, moreover, that the move-
ment was not oonfined to the working class,
but that it had the sympathy of vast numbers
of the upper and middle classes. Mr. James
Heywood then addressed the right hon gentle-
men, and argued strongly in favour of art
workmen being permitted on their only
day of leisure during the week to improve
and refine their mental and social status.
Mr. Morrell, hon. see. of the League, men-
tioned that in the last exhibition numerous
West-end tradesmen exhibited. articles which
they represented as being of English manu-
facture, whereas the fact was that, although
made in England, they were the production of
foreign workmen, who in Germany in par-
ticular, had art schools and other privileges of
the kind which they could u Wild on Sundays,
and they moreover had access to all the works
of the great masters and art treasures in the
national collections throughout the empire.
He also impressed upon the attention of the
ight hon. gentlemen that the vast majority of
working men favoured the movement. The
Marquis of Ripon promised on behalf of Mr.
Forster and himself the most careful consider-
ation of the subject, but told the deputation
that they must all feel it could not be treated
as a departmental question.lt was really a
general question involving considerations of
public policy and convenience, and it was
therefore impossible for one department or any
individual members of the Government to
deal with it, but Mr. Forster and he would
make it their duty to represent to their
colleagues the nature of the statements and
memorial laid before them, and on the part of
the Government he was sure he might say the
subject would receive every consideration.
After thanking his lordship and the vice-
president for this answer, the deputation
retired.

articles.title: WORKING MEN'S CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES.
articles.text:
WORKING MEN'S CO-OPERATIVE
SOCIETIES.

The contrast between Lancashire and York-
shire and the rest of England and Wales is
remarkable. In the seven years 1864-70 the
two northern counties invest £664,000 more
than they withdraw, but the rest of England
and Wales only £47,000. The general result
is, however, that the share capital in the two
counties in 1870 is three times as great as in
1864, and in the other counties more than
four times as great. A fertile source of the
increase of investments in shares arises from
the habit of members employing, as further
investments in the store with which they deal,
the bonuses on purchases already referred to.
We shall see more of this when we advance
further into the inquiry. . . It is clear
from the figures that since 1866 there has
been a great extension a the business of co-

operative societies. According to the imper-
fect return before us the goods sold in 1870
amounted to £8,200,000, or an average of £32
to each of the 250,000 members, and the share
capital was £2,034,000, besides £197,000 on
loan. Allowing for the societies omitting to
make returns it is within the truth to estimate
the actual sales of 1870 to all the co-operative
associations of one kind or another at nearly
l 2 millions sterling, and the capital embarked
in them as quite three millions, and the
number of members as over 300,000. . .
. . The detail of expenses as compared with
capital raised by shares and loans is
progressively favourable since 1866. Thus
the management outgoings having fallen
from 13 to 94 per cent.;. and we
see that the total expenses (including
interest on shares and loans) on goods sold has
fallen from 51 to 4 per cent. per annum.
After allowing for these expenses, there re-
mained in 1870 a net profit of 27 per cent, per
annum on the capital employed in the business,
or equal to 61; per cent, on the value of the
goods sold; and the whole of that 611 per
cent. (or, say, is. 3d. in the 1) was re-
turned, directly or indirectly, to the purchasers
of goods, with the qualification that the bonus
to members is double the rate given to
strangers; supposing, therefore, an average
purchase of £32 per annum, the bonus would
be, say, £1 18s. If from the expenses we
take away the interest on capital raised, the
cost of management in 1870 would be under
3 per cent. on the goods sold. It is difficult
to arrive at any extensive average of the ex-
penses of conducting ordinary retail business
in private shops in provincial towns. But it
is certainly very high, and we dare say that
in a large class of cases the ratio is not less
than from 15 to 20 per cent. on the amount of
goods sold. But in this high percentage there
are heavy charges for credit, bad debts, de=
livery, advertising, attractive premises and
attendance, douceurs to servants, and all the
other arts, fair and unfair, to which excessive
competition among small and large capitalists
gives rise. The co-operative stores are free
from all these drawbacks. They deal only for
ready money in all they buy and sell, and they
start with a body of customers which, under
good Management, is exactly proportioned to
their calculations and capacity. The identity of
interest also between the store and the custo-
mer is complete. The store has no inducement
to put off bad quality or bad measure, and
whatever the customer pays over and above
prime cost and expenses he gets back again in
quarterly bonus. At Rochdale these bonuses
have fur sonie time been equal to £30,000 per
annum, at Halifax to £20,000, and at Oldham
(including several cotton mills) about £50,000.
It is the regularity of these bonuses which
enables the stores so easily to raise money on
share capital. The ultimate result is, there-
fore, that according to the evidence before us,
about 300,000 heads of fumilies (almost wholly
belonging to the working classes, and includ-
ing, say, 1,200,000 persons) are at present
supplying themselves with the largest part of
the articles of domestic consumption in an-
honest and pure state at less than 3 per cent.
on the first wholesale cost. As compared with
the previous state of things, it is not an ex-
aggerated view to say that this figure repre-
sents an economy of saving in favour of the
consumer of quite 20 per cent. per annum—
that is to say, that co-operative stores, so far
as they have gone, have enabled their custo-
mers to obtain 20 per cent. more for their
money than they got before—or, say, to trans-
fer two millions per annum from the shopkeep-
ing mainly to the working olasses.—Econo-
Pnist.

articles.title: CHELSEA HALL AND CLUB ASSOCIA.TION.
articles.text:
CHELSEA HALL AND CLUB
ASSOCIA.TION.

On Wednesday evening the formation of this
society was inaugurated by a public dinner,
given in Mr. Freak's handsome building lying
off the Fulham-road, opposite Pelham-orescent.
Between 200 and 300 sat down, all belonging
to the intelligent :and well-to-do operative
class, the chair being filled by Captain Charles
Mercier; the president of the association. The
object sought is a suitable and central place
of meeting for the 'various benevolent and
friendlysocieties of the borough of Chelsea such
as the Odd Fellows, Foresters, Druids, Loan,
Buildings, Sm., which it is estimated number
not less than 70. With this view the associa-
tion was formed upon the limited liability
principle, and baa already received no small
amount of support., including contributions of
£lOO from Mr. Franks, £5O from Sir Wm.
Tito, M.P., £lO from Mr. ho. Boyd, and
£270 as subscriptions for shares of X 1 each, of
which .£l5O came from 150 working men.
Besides the place of meeting it is also proposed
to establish a social and educational club, and
to avoid misconception it is laid down as trfun-
damental rule in the articles of association
that this branch shall be entirely free from
party politics. At present the association is
allowed to use the hall in which the dinner
took place for lectures and other purposes,
without paying rent, and no doubt this con-
cession will help on the realization of the
£5,000 to £lO,OOO required to complete
the aim of its projectors, for whom Ur.

M. Walbrook, of
_Walham-green, acts
as honorary secretary. The hall on this
occasion was decorated with much taste, and
it was announced that two flags suspended
above the chairman had gone through Bfaz-
zini's and. Garibaldi's struggles for Italian
liberty. Some stains upon one of them were
referred to as marks of human blood spilt upon
the battle-field. Due justice was done to
conventional toasts, and success to the Chelsea
Hall and Club Association called forth enthu-
siastic rounds of applause. Lieutenant-Colo-
nel Hobson, Sir Alfred Slade, The Hon. Sey-
mour Egerton, Alderman F. Gould, Mr. C. .T.
Freak, Ur. J. Miller, Mr. James Nation (soli-
tor), Mr. C. Pratt, (auditor), and Mr. J. Pul-
ling occupied seats at the chairman's table.
The Marquis Townsend, who was to have
propoied the toast of the evening, Mr. Locock
Webb, the Rev. 11. Bolly, and the Rector of
Chelsea, sent written apologies for their un-
avoidable absence. The Friendly Societies, in
whose interest :the movement is chiefly made,
were most strongly represented, and many. of
their members not only. furnished the musical
portion of the entertainment, but delivered
speeches, and before the night passed away
put their names down for shares in the asso-
ciation.

TOE MAIN CHANCE.
Si,—What we all want is bread and butter,
and this can only be got by steam power. Men
are tired of manual labour._ They know steam
wall° all. They have no objection to build
and set the engines to work, whether to make
materials for buildings, or to till the ground,
or to fetch and carry, or to furnish, clothe,
feed, bathe, warm. Tho use of steam power
all over the world most economically can only
be done by selected patterns of the things or
objects required made by the million. They
must be of striotly limited forms. This is a
sine qua non. All the rest of our wants will
be supplied. easily enough when once we have
thus overcome, the drudgeries of life. Until
this is done, nothing can be done of any par.
tioular good, despite positivists, religionists,
philosophers, or philanthropists. Ruskin* is
well aware of this, or he would not have quoted
me on dna subject as he has done. In order
tá obtain this desirable end, a Committee of
Engineers must be appointed under a union of
, Governments.

WM. RIDDLE, C.E.
