articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

A number of gentlemen, recognising the
services rendered by the Lord Mayor to the
citizens of London, on Monday presented to
the Lady Mayoress a full-length portrait of
his lordship, together with a service of massive
plate.

The Select Committee upon the Government
Bill for the abolition of the truck system met
on Monday for the first time, Mr. Gathorne
Hardy in the chair. No evidence was, how-
ever, taken, the Committee having decided to
consider the measure with closed doors.

This 'year's Synod of the English Presby-
terian Church was opened on Monday evening
in Regent-square. The Rev. Thain David-
son, of Islington, was unanimously elected
Moderator for the ensuing year.

Dr. Thomas Yowler Short, who resigned
the bishopric of St. Asaph about two years
ago, has just died at the age of 83.

A telegram from Geneva announces that the
counter cases in the Alabama arbitration were
laid before the tribunal on Monday morning.
Fears are expressed lest the nature of the
British protest may prevent a settlement of the
dispute.

Official documents have been published in
Madrid, which represent that the Ministerial
majority in the Spanish Parliament will be
116, without reckoning fifteen independent
members.

Special telegrams from Paris announce that
Marguerite Dixblane was arrested, not as
originally stated in a low wine shop, but in a
cold shop, and her face was blackened like that
of a chimney sweep. Of the stolen property
£2,400 worth has been recovered, as well as
jewels and other valuables. Five persons
have been arrested as accomplices, but they are
likely to get off owing to the fact that the
principal is to be prosecuted in England, and
that the provisions of the Extradition Treaty
do not apply to their case.

Mrs. Eliza Wyld, 61 years of age, was on
Monday charged at Bow-street on suspieion of
having caused tha,death of her husband, James
Wyld, at 31, Brydges-street, Strand. The
deceased was the editor and proprietor of a
paper published in the interests of the licensed
viotuallers, and it was alleged that his death
had been caused by the violence of his wife
during a quarrel. She was remanded, two
surieties of £5O each being accepted for her
next appearance.

Several bakers were summoned at the
Lambeth Police Court on Monday for having
infringed the provisions of the Smoke Act. The
defendants complained that the statute bore
harshly upon them, and as the magistrate ex-
pressed his wish to make a personal inspection
of one of the bakeries, the proceedings were
adjourned for that purpose.

A man, named Hayes was on 'Monday charged
at the Southwark Police Court with having
caused the death of one Patrick Carroll in a
pugilistic encounter. The prisoner, who
declared that the fight was a fair one, was
remanded, substantial bail being required.

Reuniting in the army is now progressing
very slowly, and in the Royal Artillery alone
there are more than 2,000 gunners below the
proper strength of the establishment.

Easter Term was opened on Monday, after
the judges and Queen's counsel had been en-
. teamed by the Lord Chancellor, at his resi-
dence in Great George-street, 'Westminster.

A fearful tragedy was brought to light on
Monday afternoon at 16,Copland-street, Maida-
hill. A shoemaker named. Nicholls, 46 years
of age, during the temporary absence of his
wife, murdered four of his children, and then
committed suicide. The victims were—Eliza
Nicholls, aged nine years; Itosina, five;
Louisa, three; and James Henry, 14 months.
There are two other children, but fortunately
they were not in the house at the time. It is
stated that the wretched man has shown symp-*
toms of insanity for several weeks past.

A firm of foreign goods importers, carrying
on business in Houndsditoh, were on Monday
prosecuted by:the Great Eastern Railway Com-
pany for having sent by rail a ease of detona-
ting compound of an inflammable- character,
tinder the pretence that the box contained
hardware only. The hearing, which came
before the Lord Mayor at the Mansion-house,
was ultimately adjourned to admit of the proof
of the company's bye-laws.

A. cook, bearing the name of Abigail Thames
was on the 12th brought up at the Southwark
Police Court charged with having, whilst in a
state of intoxication, assaulted her master, a
surgeon in practice in the Jamaica-road, Ber-
mondsey. She was sentenced to two months'
imprisonment, with hard labour.

On the 12th inst. a destructive fire occurred
at the extensive chemical works of Mr. W.
Mather, Cornbrook, Manchester. When the
Manchester fire brigade arrived they found a
large range of buildings of a triangular form
in flames, and some hours elapsed before the
efforts of the fire brigade were successful in
subduing the flames. The damage extends
over a considerable portion of the premises,
and the loss is estimated at between £7,000
and £B,OOO. It is not known how the fire
originated.

Brazil has had great rejoicing over the
return of its Emperor and Empress. They
were enthusiastically received at Pernambuco
and Bahia; but the national welcome was
being arranged for at:Rio de Janiero.

Generous and satisfactory terms of peace
have been granted to Paraguay. Brazil
guarantees for five years the independence of
the subjugated State, and accepts a general
acknowledgment of liability for the expenses
of the war.

Dr. Norris, president of Corpus Christi
College, died on Tuesday morning, after a few
weeks illness. He had been head of the
college since 1842.

A. Biennial Male Scholarship in the Royal
Academy of Music, and an annual prize for a
female student at the same Academy, form
the proposed application of the Sterndale
Bennett testimonial. The subscriptions now
exceed £l,OOO.

In the Court of Probate Lord Penzance has
refused an application by the defendant in a
suit instituted by the Claimant in 1868 for
the revocation of Sir Roger Tichborne's will,
to send the case for trial by a separate jury.
Mr. Bayford, in making the application, said
that it was not intended to proceed with it
until the issue of the proceedings now pending
against the Claimant.

Godriola v. Godrich" has reduced itself to
two issues—one of adultery, charged against
the respondent, and the other of costs. Lord
Penzance lurs taken time to consider a motion
that it be again set down for hearing.

A. statement made by the French Minister
of the Interior to the Permanent Committee,
implies that negotiations are in progress with
the German Government relative to the alleged
expulsion of Alsatians choosing French na-
tionality.

After a stormy, and at times, chaotic ses-
sion, the Hungarian Diet has been prorogued.
The Emperor-King
i commented rather signifi-
cantly n his speech on the number of con-
stitutional questions which had been settled
without disagreement. He congratulated the
Diet on its share in that work, and specified
the principal judicial and administrative re-
forms it had effected. He announced, also, a
much improved state of finance, and augured
hopefully of tho future.

Madrid has elected four Ministerial Sena-
tors, with Marshal Espartero at the head of
the poll. The other three were, however, close
run by the highest of the Opposition candi-
dates. The returns from twenty-five provinces
are said to show 22 in favour of the Govern-
ment. The totals so far are 113 Ministerialists
against 39 Opposition Senators.

With one exception, the Carlists risings
have subsided as abruptly as they originated.
The surviving band has made offers of submis-
sion, and the whole project is pronounced a
failure.

Senor de Bias has, it is said, obtained a
cordial response to his circular about the In-
ternational. Several foreign Ministers have
assured him of the intention of their respective
Governments to use repressive measures
against the society.

James Trooper, a diver, of Liverpool, died
suddenly at Pichidangui, while employed in
raising the cargo of a sunken vessel at Cape
Horn. The vessel was sunk in 33i fathoms of
water. He had been down to the wreak four
times the previous day, and on the day of his
death he had just come up from being down
32 minutes, and was about to dive again. He
complained of a pain in the small of his back,
and died in about ten minutes.

It is state& that a gentleman in Limerick
has received a letter from a friend residing in
Wagga-Wagga, in which the writer positively
states that there can be no doubt as to the
identity of the claimant; that Arthur Orton
is at present, and has been for some time hid-
ing in the bush, where he was lately seen by
several persons who knew him in Wagga-
Wagga.

From the is to the 13th instant the Trea-
sury receipts amounted to £2,893,923, and the
expenditure to £6,3.11,377. The balance in
the Bank of England on Saturday last was
£4,705,937.

A special telegram, by Atlantic cable, from
New York, states that Professor Woolsey, one
of the highest American authorities on inter-
national law, recommends that the claims for
indirect damages should be withdrawn, on the
ground that they are not justified by the terms
of the Washington Treaty.

Thiers has addressed a letter to King
Amadeo, in which he states that no Power,
including even Italy, has a greater interest
than France in the consolidation of the
dynasty and institutions of Spain. We learn
from Madrid that a few Carlist bands still
keep up an agitation in the country, but that
they disperse at sight of the troops. In the
province of Barcelona there is now, it is said,
but a single band, and it is so completely dis.
couraged that it is willing to surrender.

The report of the progress of the Ordnance
survey for the past year has been issued. It
states that the plans of London on the Beale of
60 inches to a mile are now complete. They
are drawn on 326 full-sized sheets of paper,
and probably form the largest and most com-
plete plan of a Oily ever produced. Of these
plans, 144 sheets have been engraved and pub-
lished, and the remainder are in progress. The
continual increase in the size of London and
the alterations constantly made in it are so
great as to make it highly desirable that
arrangements should be made for an almost
constant revision of the plans. This has been
represented to the Metropolitan Board of
Works, and the Board, in reply, state that there
are no funds legally applicable to this service;
but they fully appreciate the importance of
keeping the survey always complete.

From the Registrar-General's return for the
past week we learn that during the week
ending Saturday last 5,800 births and 3,712
deaths were registered in London and twenty
other large °Wes and towns of the United king.
dom. The aggregate mortality in these towns
was at the rate of' 26 deaths annually to every
1,000 persons. In London itself 2,574 births
and 1,470 deaths were registered last week,
and the death rate had declined from 26 and 23
in previous weeks to 23 per 1,000.

Two writs of sequestration were on Sunday
morning exhibited upon the doors of Leaming-
ton parish church. The vicar, however, who
has lately been charged with insobriety, con-
ducted the service as usual.

It is stated in a Paris telegram that there
is no foundation for the rumour of French
troops having been concentrated on the Italian
frontier, and that no representations on the
subject of Nice have been made by Italy to
France. The relations between the two
countries, it is added, are perfectly satisfac-
tory.

A correspondent writes that nightingales
have been singing at Bromley, Kent, since the
2nd instant. This date is unusually early, as
in former years they have not been heard before
the 14th April.

Mr. Justice Brett heard an application on
Saturday for the admission of the Tiokborne
Claimant to bail. An affidavit was made by
his solicitor, Mr. F. G. Gorton, which stated
that he was prepared with sureties to a reason-
able amount, and that he believed, from an
examination of the documents connected with
the case, that the prisoner had a good defence
to all the charges made against him. It was
almost impossible properly to get up the defence
unless the Claimant had constant access to
his legal adviser. His lordship held that this
was not a sufficient reason for his acceding to
the application, inasmuch as Mr. Gorton could
see the claimant in Newgate whenever he
thought proper. He therefore declined to make
Any order.

The April sessions of the Central Criminal
Court were brought to a close on Saturday,
when several cases were disposed of before Air.
Commissioner Kerr. Charles Westhorp, upon
being convicted of a brutal assult upon a
woman who had passed as his wife, was sen-
tenced to four months' imprisonment. John
Joyce, for a robbery with violence, was ordered
to be kept in penal servitude for seven years,
and to receive forty lashes with the "cat."

Tho Galway election inquiry was again
resumed on Saturday. Amongst the witnesses
was a Mr. Henderson, one of the solicitors
engaged for Captain Nolan, who deposed that
neither intimidation nor undue influence was
used on behalf of, the sitting member.

From the account published ty the Gironde
of a terrible murder of five persons at Barp,
near Bordeaux, it appears that the crime was
committed on Tuesday night, but was not dis-
covered until the next morning. The house
was occupied by the postman of the district,
who was away at the time. The persons mur-
dered were his father-in-law, his mother-in-
law, his wife, and two of his children, one of
whom. was tivo years of age, and the other only
sixteen months. Two elder children in an ad-
joining room escaped.

APRIL 20, 1872.

An International Exhibition is to be opened
in Lima in December, and on Saturday evening
a number of gentleman interested in the
project dined at the Cannon-street Hotel.
The administration of the Peruvian President,
Colonel Jose Balta, was warmly praised. Th,
Exhibition atwas to have been opened in
December last, but owing to the great de-
wand for space, it was, by desire of the Govern-
ment, postponed to May next.

There has been a large meeting in New
York of Republicans who are opposed to the
re-election of President Grant. Mr. Horace
Greely, Mr. Schurz, and Mr. Trumbull took
part in the proceedings. A coalition between
the Democrats and the Republicans hostile to
President Grant is predicted.

Scholarships, open to boys under 14, have
been awarded at Halley bury College as
follows :—Williams; £3O; Hallward, £3O;
Wheeler, £2O. Honourably mentioned :
Jellieoe and Hughes; the two last being
members of the school.

A boy of 13, named Stanton' has been killed
by an elephant at Hanley. Messrs. Bostock
and Wombwell's Menagerie arrived at this town
on Saturday, and among the animals was an
elephant, which was taken to an inn stable.
A number of children gathered in the inn.
yard, and amused themselves by giving the
elephant nuts, and other things. 801110 of
them are said to have given it stones, at which
the animal was so irritated, that he seized the
deceased child with his trunk, and raised hiui-.
to his mouth; a keeper, seeing what was
occurring, called out, and the animal dropped
the child. He was picked up and at once
taken to a doctor, and although every effort
was made to restore him, he died on Monday
night from wounds in the head and severe
internal injuries.

The attention of visitors to the Inner Tem-
ple garden during the past few days has been
attracted by the magnificent show of tulips
displayed there, and which are now in full
bloom. The recent snow has somewhat re-
tarded the perfection of the finest specimens,
notwithstanding the utmost care has been
taken by Mr. Newton, gardener to the hon..
society. Amongst the most notable exhibited
may be enumerated the Imperator Rubrum, a
brilliant orange red; Moller°, a fine purple,
with yellow base; Keizerskroon, yellow and
red, similar to Tournesol (double), of which
two beds have a very pretty effect.

A singular disease has broken out among
the dogs in some parts of Shropshire. They
exhibit great restlessness, and on being opened
a black fluid is found in the stomach, which
is much inflamed. John Jordan, a farm
bailiff, residing near Stanton Long, has been
bitten by one of these dogs. The affected
piece was cut out by a surgeon, but the man .
lies in a most precarious condition.

The Peabody trustees have decided to erect
several blocks of buildings in Bermondsey,
similar to those in the Blaokfriars-road,
and have proceeded with the erection of
the first block, the site for which is in East-
street, near New Church.street, and in con-
nection with the intended building the Ber-
mondsey local authorities are endeavouring to
secure the making of a new and improved
thoroughfare between East-street and New
Churob-street.

In the report of the Endowed Schools.
Commissioners, which has just been presented;
to the Education Department, the fornier.
.defend the course which they have taken iii.
the appointment of trustees to the several
promulgated schemes. No preponderance has
been given to any one party, whether in civil .
or in ecolesiastical politics, but each group of
trustees has been chosen for the good of its
own endowment, and with reference solely to.
legal and educational considerations. The
Commissioners admit that they have disturbed.
a large number of interests, traditions, and,
sentiments, but they contend quit strong,
measures era required in clealing with the.
great and accumulated evils which had.
gathered round many of our ancient endow-
ments.

A telegram from Exeter says a strange dis-
tarbanee took place there on Saturday evening.
The volunteer engineers Were engaged in blow-
ing up a disused brick kiln, and several
thousand persons were present. The gates of
the field were barred against the crowd, but
they broke them down and made a rush for
admittance. The guard fired his carbine over
their heads and brought his bayonet to the
charge. Several hundred people got past, and
the rest of the engineers came to the rescue of
the guard. They attempted to force back the
mob, and then sticks and stones were thrown
freely. Fighting cantinued for some time and.
one of the engineers was severely wounded in
the face by a blow from a brickbat. The
engineers were at length marched oif, leaving
the mob masters of the pusiti:Ju. As the
volunteers marched back to their head-quarters
they were followed by the mob, who violently
hissed thorn.

Another case of ill-treating a child came before
the Clerkenwell magistrate on Tuesday. Amelia
Conway was charged with beating her .step-
child, Fanny Conway, aged nine years, with a
thick stick, the father himself having begged the
neighbours to interfere, and prevent the little
one from being killed. The child was not
sworn, as she was found to be quite ignorant
of the nature of an oath; but the woman was
sentenced to a month's hard labour.

William Kittle, and Ellen, his wife, charged
at Colchester with poisoning Elizabeth Kittle,
the former wife of the male prisoner, by
administering arsenic, were again remanded
by the magistrates at Mistley on Tnesday.
The body had been exhumed, and arsenic
found in the intestines.

Intelligence received at Greenock states that
the Newfoundland seal fisheries have not been
so successful as last year, owing to the heavy
packed ice at the fishing ground, which pre-
vented the vessels from getting among the
seals; one steamer is reported with three
propellers broken; and another steamer
is reported as in a dangerous position.
The Kingfisher (sailing vessel) had been
lost; crew saved; the weather had been
stormy, but by the last accounts was more
settlea. The Woolf (s.), of Greenock, is re-
ported with 11,000; her master states that
about 80,000 seals had been hauled on shore
by natives. The Bloodhound (s), of Greenock,
is reported with 16,000 seals.

An inquest was held on Tuesday afternoon
at the Vestry-hall, St. Martin-in-the-Fields,
before Mr. Bedford, coroner, on the body of
James Wyld, editor and proprietor of the
Licensed Victuallers' Guardian, who met his
death under circumstances resulting in the
apprehension of his wife and reported in our
columns elsewhere. Medical evidence was
adduced, showing that the deceased went about
his avocations some time after the injury, and
that there was no connection between the
wound and the cause of his death, which was
fatty degeneration of the heart. Verdict:—
"Died from natural causes."

The polling at Tamworth took place on
Tuesday, when Mr. Ilanbury, the Conserva-
tive candidate, was returned by 966 votes
against 319 recorded for Sir Spencer Robinson.

---
There was an animated discussion at the
Court of Aldermen on TueEday, on the alleged
disrespect to that body, as shown in the absence
of both sheriffs from their official places. It
was explained that Sir F. Truscott was con-
fined to his bed by an attack of illness, and Sir
D. Salomons expressed an opinion that the
sheriffs had been rebuked somewhat hastily.

The marriage of the Marquis of Bute to the
Hon. Gwendaline Mary Arnie, eldest daughter
of Lord Howard of Glossop, was solemnised. on
Tuesday at the Oratory, Brompton, in the
presence of a numereus and distinguished
gathering. Archbishop Manning was the
officiating prelate. The marriage register
VS signed by the Duke of Cambridge, the
Duke of Northumberland, the Duke of Argyll,
and Mr. Disraeli. The Holy Communion
having been administered to the newly-wedded
couple, they were addressed by Monsignor
Capel, who briefly reminded them of the
responsibilities which they had taken upon
themselves, 3 and exhorted theta amid tho
changing scenes of life, to make their home a
model of Christian perfection, The Marquis
and Marchioness, left for Cardiff in the after-
noon.

• Deputations, beaded respectively by Sir
Charles Dilke, M.P., and Mr. Harvey Lewis,
M.P., on Tuesday waited upon the Marquis of
Ripon, to urge the opening of the British
Museum and other art galleries to the public
on Sundays. The Lord President of the
Council promised, on behalf of Mr. Forster
and himself, carefully to consider the subject.
it could not, however, be treated as a depart-
mental question, hut as involving one of public
polioy, and for this reason his colleagues must
be consulted before a definitive reply was
made.

On Tuesday the annual meeting of the clergy
and churchwardens of the diocese of London
was held, the object being the promotion of
the Fund established by the' present Arch-
bishop of Canterbury. It was stated that a
sum of £435,000 had been promised or
received, and that, in addition to this amount,
£840,000 had within the past few years been
raised within the diocese for church and
school purposes.

An application was made on Monday to Lord
Penzance that the suit of Tichborne v. (losford,
which was entered for hearing nearly four
years ago, might now be tried by a special
jury. The defendant, it will be remembered,
was the executor to the will made by Roger
'Pichborne before he left England onw bat the
family consider his last voyage. His lordship,
however, held that as matters at present stood
with respect to the claimant, it would be
advisable to make no order.

It is stated in a telegram from Florence
that the majority of the merchants there are
in favour of Free Trade. The Industrial
inquiry, which has been going on for some
time in Florence, with the view of ascertaining
in what manner the resources of Italy may
best be developed, has now terminated. Its
next sittings will be held in Milan, and after-
wards in Venice and Palermo.

On Tuesday the official correspondence
respecting the presentation to the Geneva
Tribunal of the British Counter Case in the
Alabama arbitration was laid before Parlia-
ment. The correspondence consists of a
despatch from Lord Granville to Sir E.
Thornton, another from Earl Granville to
General Schenck, General Schenck's reply,
and the declaration of the British Govern-
ment sent in to the arbitrators on Monday last.
The declaration explains that a misunderstand-
ing has arisen between Great Britain and the
United States with regard to the claims for
indirect damages which claims are not ad-
mitted by her Majesty's Government to be
"within either the scope or the intention of the
reference to arbitration." Her Majesty's Go-
vernment has, nevertheless, thought it proper
to present its Counter Case without preku.dice,
and under the express reservation of all
rights "in the event of a difference con-
tinuing to exist between the high contract-
ing parties as to the scope and inten-
tion of the reference to arbitration."
General Schenck bad stated to Lord Granville
on the sth inst. that his Government con-
sidered the British Government was bound
under the terms of the Treaty to file a Counter
Case, and that by doins so it would not pre-
judice its position or afteet that of the United
States, but that the right of both parties would
be the same after filing as before.

At a meeting of the Southampton Indepen-
dent Ratepayers' Protection Association, held
on Tuesday last, Mr. Knowles in the chair,
the following resolution was proposed by Mr.
W. M. Kill, seconded by Mr. Saunders, and
carried unanimously, "That this meeting
tenders its sincere and hearty thanks to Mrs.
Fawcett for her noble, patriotic, and eloquent
lecture in advocacy of the enfranchisement of
her sex, which lecture was given by her at the
Philharmonic-hall, on Monday, April Bth,
1872," The Ron. Secretary, Mr. Briggs, was
requested to forward this resolution to Mrs.
Fawcett.

The judges in the Fine Arts have raised the
standard this year much higher than in 1871.
Out of sixteen hundred works subMitted, only
about six hundred have been accepted. Among
the British pictures will be found Millais' first
exhibited oil painting, executed when he was
about 16 years of age ; also Frith's "Railway
Station."

The business of the English Presbyterian
Synod was again proceeded with on Wednes •
day, the Rev. Thaia Davidson, the new
Moderator, presiding.

The half-yearly meeting of the Solicitors'
Benevolent Association was held on Wednes-
day, when a report containing many satisfac-
tory features was presented.

In the ease of Messrs. Hyam, who were pro-
secuted by the Great Eastern Railway Com-
pany for having sent a dangerous compound
by rail with an imperfect description of the
same, explanations have been made, and the
proceedings now stand adjourned for three
months.

Last week the total number of paupers in
the metropolis was 113,593, of whom 34,244
were in workhouses, and 79,349 received out-
door relief. Compared with tlae correspond-
ing week last year, this was a decrease of
19,854. The total number of vagrants re-
lieved was 873.

Vice-Chancellor Wiokens lately granted an
'injunction, at the suit of the proprietor of the
Swindon Refreshment-rooms, restraining the
Grata Western Railway Company from run-
ning an up and a down tram daily which
stopped at Swindon five minutes only, instead
of ten, according to a covenant that all trains
should stop the longer period. The company,
pleading the authority of the Postmaster
-
General for the step which they took, appealed
to the full Court—consisting of the Lord
Chancellor and the Lords Justices—which
on Wednesday overruled the decision of the
Court 'below.

Under the Pensions Commutation dot of
1869 an Admiralty dark named Jones, who
had been dismissed from her Majesty's service
several years previously, obtained £2,200 from
the Treasury by representing that his half-pay
allowance amounted to £195 per annum. The
fact was that he had repeatedly applied for
employment under the Crown from the time
of his dismissal, and that he had met with
constant refusals. The Attorney-General,
therefore, filed a bill against him for the
recovery of the mono', and Vice-Chancellor
Bacon on Wednesday ordered Mr. Jones to
repay it, with interest at 4 per cent.

Mr. Edwin James, formerly a Queen's
Counsel at the English bar, on Wednesday
night lectured at St. George's-hall on his ten
years' 'experience in the United States.

The widow of a man who had been in the
service of the Rev. It. C. Halpin, Chaplain to
the Forces, was on Wednesday summoned at
the Hampstead Police-court for having detained
a livery coat worn by her late husband, valued
at 40$. The defendant urged that, as her
husband had worn the garment two summers,
she had a just claim to it; but the Bench
ordered her to give it up, and to pay 55.
costs.

The inquest upon the victims of the Maida-
hill tragedy was opened and concluded on
Wednesday, when the widow of the unfor-
tunate man Nicholls and one of the surviving
children were amongst the witnesses before the
Coroner's Court. The jury found that
Nicholls was in an unsound state of mind
when he murdered his children and put an end
to his own exiatenos.

On Wednesday the Court of Queen's Bench
granted a rule nisi, calling upon the Treasury
to show cause why the claimant to the TiCh-
borne baronetcy should not be admitted to bail.

Police-constable Elton, of the S division,
was on Wednesday convicted at the Middlesex
Sessions of having assaulted a young man in
High-street, Camden Town, on the evening of
Thanksgiving-day. The judge ordered him to
enter into his recognizances to come up for
sentence if called upon, and intimated his in-
tention of recommending that the man should
be retained in the force.

Frederick James, ,a boot sewer, was again
brought up at Worship-street on Wednesday,
charged with the wilful murder of Charles
Starkie, by shooting him through the bead
with a revolver. Re was committed for trial.

Thomas Hayes, a glass-blower, was on
Wednesday committed from the Southwark
Police Court on a charge of manslaughter, the
specific allegation being that he had caused the
death of one Patrick Carroll in a prize light.

It is announced from Bayonne that muni-
tions of war, intended for the Spanish
conspirators, have been seized at the French
frontier, and that French troops are on the
watch there. From Madrid we learn that the
only Catalonian band still at large, atter being
closely pursued, has escaped into the province
of Barcelona. Another band has seized the
communal funds of a small village, and left a
receipt for it in the name of the " General
Commanding-in-Chief of the Federal Armies
of Don Carlo,."

The Paris .Radical expresses great admira-
tion for the Times article on the Warwiok.shire
strike, and the fairness with which that journal
states the case for the labourers, in spite of
what the French paper considers its Conserva-
tive prejudices. "If such a strike took place
in France, says the .Radical, "a law would be
passed to-morrow against farm-servants as a
law was passed but yesterday against the
International. Discussion precedes judgment
in England; in France but one voice is heard,
that of passion; whosoever claims a right,
when that right forms our privilege, is our
enemy. The farm-servants do not find that
everything is for the best in this best of all ,
possible worlds. The English say: It is '
possible; let us discuss the matter ! The
French proprietors would say: "They are
insurgents ! let us adopt severe meaaures I"
Their opinion of French toleration is borne out
by a denunciatory article in the Constitutionnel,
in which the following sentence occurs
"After the incendiaries of Paris, you would
have a Jacquine in the departments, neo-
Robespierres of the farm, neo-Marats of the
hamlet." The article, however, acknowledges
that the agricultural labourers on strike are
not a source of danger to England. "Why
not?" rejoins the _Radical. Because the
English donservatives do not call in an armed
force, because they, do not ask for courts-
martial, because they do not make exceptional
laws against them. Steitin in the open air is
powerless. The violence of the explosion is in
proportion to the amount of compression."

In the Belgian Chamber some explanations
have been given by the Minister for Foreign
Affairs, the purport of which was to show that
no differnces existed between Italy and
Belgium. It was admitted, however, by the
Minister that certain points had been discussed
by the two Governments, and a note sent to
the Belgian representative in Rome. To that
note no answer had been received. This reply did
not appear to satisfy the House, and a debate
followed. Ultimately, a motion for the pro-
duction of correspondence on the subject was
negatived by M votes against 41.

A man named Thomas Arthur, of Old
Swindon, while out with his wife for a drive,
beat her to death for becoming intoxicated,
drove the body home, and was at once taken
into custody,

articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.
The Constitutionnel positively contradicts the
assertions of the Daily Telegraph that com-
plications exist between France and Ger-
many.

The charge of murder against William and
Ellen Kittle, for poisoning the male prisoner's
wife, in October last, was brought to a close
yesterday. The magistrates committed the
female prisoner on the capital charge and
discharged her husband. Bail refused.
The Enchantress, with the remains of Lord
Mayo, is expected to arrive at the North Wall,
Dublin, on or about the 24th inst.

It is said that the police have at present no
definite information as to the time at which

Marguerite -Diablano will arrive in this
country. Any report to the contrary is un-
authentic.

It is understood that Sir George Grey
declines to accept the position of Chairman of
the Committe on the Game Laws, principally
on the grounds of health; and Arr. Ward
Hunt, it is thought likely, will be chosen to
fill the post.
It is said that the O'Conor Don, M.P., in a
letter to the Secretary of the Roscommon Home
tiovernment Association, has expressed his
determination to support the principles of
Rome Rule.

The Birmingham operative bakers have
threatened to strike unless they receive an
advance of wages to an amount which would

be covered, it i stated, by raising the price of
bread to the public one halfpenny per 41b. loaf.
Last night 115 poor emigrants, assisted by
the Clerkenwell Emigration Society, started for
Canada. This philanthropic society has now
aided 2,445 poor people, the majority of whom
are doing well in Canada.

According to the Washington correspon-
dence of several New York journals, it is
reported that the Administration has decided
to withdraw the claims for indirect damages.
Western Australia has been visited by a
severe cyclone; and the Theatre Royal, Mel-
bourne, has been destroyed by tire.
The o.lfitiel Gazette of Madrid publishes a
decree granting a concession for laying two
submarine telegraph cables, one from Englan d
the other from Portugal, and terminating at a
point yet to be determined on the coast of
Galicia in Spain.
The post of President of Coraus Christi
College, is likely to be conferred upon the
Rev. J. Matthias Wilson' M.A., dean of the
College! and Professor of Moral Philosophy in
the University.
Henry_ Miller, a young man, was brought
before Mr. Lushington, yesterday, charged
with attempting to shoot Charlotte Stoboll, a
young woman living at No. 43, Christian-
street, St. George's-in-the-East, and with
attempting to commit suicide by shooting
himself. The young woman had retailed to
marry him, and in a fit of desperation he
committed this rash act. He was remanded.
At Westminster, on Thursday, Mr. William
Haynes, greengrocer, of Churton-street; Pim-
lico, Mr. Joseph Haynes of Tachbrook-street,
Mr. Haylook, of Vauxhall-road, and other
tradesmen, were summoned by Inspector
Turpin, of the B division, for unlawfully
exposing vegetables, Sm., on barrows in the
carriage-way and on the pavement. Several
were fined, and others bound over.
A violent storm burst over Leeds yesterday,
accompanied by hail, rain, and a remarkable
flash of lightning, followed by a tremendous
peal of thunder. The mill chimney of Messrs.
Rishworth Brothers, corn millers, Sykes-place,
York-street: was struck by the lightning, and
the main gas-pipe broken. The escaped gas
ignited, and the woodwork was set on fire, but
the flames were extinguished before much
damage was done.
I fire, which has destroyed from £15,000 to
£20,000 worth of property, broke out yesterday
in Edinburgh, and raged for severarhours, in
the tanning and currying premises of Mr. Hugh
Brown, St. Mary-street, who possessed one of
the largest businesses of that kind in Scotland.
The fire arose through an escape of gas.
The man who presented himself at Scotland
-
yard the other night, and stated that he WO
an accomplice in the murder of Madame -Rid,
said his name was Lewis, but refused to give
his address. He persisted in his statement,
and was sent in the custody of an officer to

A. painful sensation was caused at London
Bridge Railway Station on Wednesday morn-
ing on the arrival of the 9.30 train from Green-
wich, by the removal from one of thaj third-
class carriages of the body of an elderly man,
who expired on the journey from Greenwich
to Spa-road. It appears that shortly after the
train started from Deptford, the deceased was
seen to fall forward, and with a deep groan
expired. The man was unknown to any of
his fellow paseengero, ,

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAX.
THE 13ALLOT BILL.

The proceedings of the House of Commons
commented with an interesting discussion as

HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY.
THE NEW LICENSING BILL.

Lard Kimberly brought forward the Govern-
ment plan for the amendment of the Law of
Licensing. He began by accounting for the
subject having been transferred from the Com-
mous to that House by a reference to the state
of business in the former; so that, in order to
prevent any notion that no measure was pre-
pared, it Was now brought forward, The com-
plexity of the question Was dwelt upon, and no
less than twelve different kinds of licences
granted under different laws were enumerated.
The connection of the subject with the morality
of the country was adverted to; and. the pro-
posals to deal with the sale of liquor, the Per-
missive Bill, and the Permissive Prohibitory
Bill, and the strong interests connected with
the liquor trade, were mentioned. He practi-
cally declared against the principle of the pro-
hibitory measures' but held that the sale of
liquor could not be left wholly unrestrained.
The present system being a regulated
monopoly, the point was how to deal with
it so as to amend its errors. The measure
whielf ho was to propose was not an
ambitious one; and the first matter was
the modification of the existing licenses. With
regard to newlicences; they would be granted by
magistrates in petty sessions, not to be -valid
till confirmed by a special committee appointed
at quarter sessions, In boroughs where there
were on lynnej nstices they would grantlicenoss,
and where there were more than nine, that
would be done by a committee chosen out of
the whole number, validity being gained only
through confirmation by the whole body; but.
in all cases the approval of the Secretary of
State would be necessary to ultimate validity.
The same system wottld be applied to the
metropolis. In regard to renewal of licenses, •
there would be no change in the existing
jurisdiction. Although it was not proposed
that the ratepayers should have any special
control in regard to licensing, it was intended
to enable any ratepayer to appear and object
to a licence and also to carry his opposition to
appeal, and compensation for trouble and loss
Would ho awarded in such ease. Notice of
Opposition and the nature of the evidence to
be adduced would have to be given. As to
police regulations, a register of houses and
offences committed therein is to be kept,
and after a certain number of offences had
been committed the licence would be for-
feited. More Stringent provision would be
made againstpermission of drunkenness on pro-
mises. In cases of harbouring thieves and
prostitutes, the onus of proving that persons
were not of that character would be put on
the keepers of houses. Adulteration was next
taken up, and the various substances used by.
publicans for this purpose set forth, some of
which as described Were of a very singular .
character; while it was stated, from evidence
in the matter, that most beer-drinkers did not
like beer as it came from the brewers. Provi-
sions against adulteration would be inserted
in the bill. With regard to the hours of
closing public-houses the following arrange-
rnents were stated :—ln the metropolis, houses
Would be open from seven in the morning to
twelve at night; in towns of more than ten
thousand inhabitants, from seven to eleven;
and in all other places, .from seven to ten on
week days. On Sundays, in the metropolis,
they would be open from one to three, and
closed from then till six, remaining open till
eleven; while in other places the dosing at
night would be at ten and nine. An adequate
system of inspection would be adopted. 'rites°

it was stated to be one of eensiderable detail,
and it was hoped that the measure would tend
to cheek the multiplication of public-houses
and other evils of the present system. The

FRENCH IRRIGATION COMPANY
(LIMITED).
To the Editor of the BBE-HIVE.
81R,-Will you permit me to address the
few following remarks to the English share-
holders in the above company :
Gentlemen,-11.aving received a notice of
a meeting called in Paris, for the 27th April,
by circular without signature, I called at the
office of the English Directors (who, as you
are aware, are also the liquidators of the old
Company) for an explanation to the question
of Why is there no signature to the circu-
lar ? "

The answer is—" Oh that is the French
way of doing it."
To the question—" Why have the English
shareholders not been called together in ac-
cordance with the terms of which they were
induced to part with their old shares for con-
version into new, and a statement of aecounts
and balance-sheet put into their hands 14 days
before the meeting at Paris everS, year, ,so that
they might have data for judging as to how to
proceed with regard to attending the Paris
general meeting, whether by proxy or other-
wise?"—the answer is—" I was not aware that
the liquidators, were bound to do this."
To the question--," Is the liquidation of the
old company complete, and the accounts
clo.sed ? "—the answer is no I. the auditors have
only, just finished their audit.
The question—" Why so long after date ? "
Answer—" Because we have not go in all
the assets yet, and. one of the liquidators is
away from home." -
The question—`-‘ Whore is Thomas Cave,
Esq., M.P." •
Answer—" He is in Italy." The .account
and balance-sheet is not in my hands, but I
will enter your name as an applicant, and
when, ready will forward you, a copy.
Such is the substance of the conversation
between./ your humble servant and, the clerk in
charge at the London office of the Company.
What the end will be is for the shareholders

APRIL 20, 1872.

to judge, and when I have placed this inferrn
mation in their hands, I consider I have
perfdrmed as far as possible my duty as a
neighbour.—l remain, yours respectfully,

TIMM- A.S BRIGGS.

We have also received the annexed com-
munication, which the writer addresses to the
shareholders in the same company :
Gentlemen,—Having received a notice of a
meeting called in Paris on April 27, 1872; by
circular, without signature, of the French
Company to whom the above company was
transferred, I feel it my duty to call the atten-
tion of my brother shareholders to the fact that
the contract under which they consented to such
transfer, has been violated. It was stipulated
in the articles agreed to by the directors of the
old company and sanctioned by the share-
holders, that a meeting should be called in
London each year in April, previous to the
annual meeting held in Paris. That a balance
sheet and report should be sent to each English
shareholder who should apply at the London
office; also a register of the shareholders should
be produced on request. At a meeting held
at the City Terminus, December 20, 1869, it
was proposed by F. Mowatt, Esq., that the
liquidators should be Thomas Cave, Esq.,
M.P., and A. Young, Esq., who, in addition to
£5OO a year each for their services, should
receive a gift of a hundred shares each, and
further stated that the liquidation would only
last a few months, when proper accounts
should he rendered to the shareholders. Years
have now passed, and no accounts have been
rendered, the liquidation is still open and if
any funds exist no doubt the liquidators are/
being paid £5OO a year. These gentlemen are
directors of the new company with their pro-
poser, F. Mowatt, Esq., to whose tender
mercies the poor unfortunate shareholders
appear to be left. It is quite true that com-
plications have taken place in France and
legal proceedings have been taken by Mr.
Fox, but these have long since ceased, and if
they had been disposed of, the liquidators
would long since have given an account of
their stewardship, and acted in accordance
with the articles of association agreed to for
the new company.

THE LONDON COACHMAKERS AND THE
NINE HOURS MOVEMENT.
To the Editor of the Bsp-Hrve.
Srn,—As a member of the same London
Society to which Mr. Whitbourn belongs, I
beg leave to repudiate such imbecile ideas as he
has thought fit to favour you with, and which
appeared in your last week's issue. I beg to
say that Mr. W. was not in any way author-
ised to speak for our or any other London
society; his audacity in so doing is scarcely
credible. Had he confined himself to answer-
ing Mr. McNay!s very pertinent. letter, and
which I felti grateful for, I should have
contentedly remained silent, well knowing
that he would be signally worsted in the
encounter; but his (Mr. W.'s) are not argu-
ments; they are deliberate misrepresentations
and insults to his fellow-man' whioh, I am
advised (wisely perhaps) to treat with the
silent scorn and contempt which they deserve,
and which I should gladly do had such ob-
servations not been published. Silence, under
such circumstances, seems to me a oritne to
ourselves and to the community; and I trust
that you are before this time inundated with
letters expressive of just indignation at such
a wanton attack. I feel that Mr. W. and
the few seeming friends Who have encouraged
him to pen such childish utterances—for
there are not any ideas in the letter—
deem his statements as final and not to
be answered, for that is the style of such men;
and truly they are unworthy of a reply, but I
cannot help asking him why he did not attempt
to show the " harm " or injury to the public,
which he says the adoption of the nine lionrs
per day would inflict? He goes on to express
the great difficulty lie has laid out for himself,
and fully admits the helplessness of the Lon-
don trade to realise that which I—whilst at
work in the country—and our country
brethren enjoy and fully appreciate. I must
here say that many country employers refuse
to give the hours until London does. Mr.
W. goes out of his way to attack the United
Kingdom Society, and complains of "restraints
which that Society imposes upon its mem-
bers;" he also asserts that they interfere be-
tween employers and employed, therein ex-
hibiting ignorance of the working of that
Society. I, and all uthers, are as free to work
at any figure or wage as Mr. W. is, and I
could name men in all the large towns who
receive wages according to their capacity.
but what would Mr. W. think of me if I were
to come to his employer and offer to make
bodies at a lower price than he is getting?
He, by his subservient talk, shows that him-
self and those "senior members" would im-
mediately make use of the power of our
London Society, and also that of the United
Kingdom Society—which, I am glad to say,
he could do in such a ease —ro drive me
from the shop, and to "black" me throughout
the trade, which every tradesman dual wher-
ever he can, Mr. Coachbuilder" included.
I arn Mr. W.'s senior member in the London
Society, and an glad to say lie does not repre-
sent us nor yet me "juniors." W. W. would

rI:;7 t
APRIL 20, 1872

lead you to infer (and this is an inference
which Mr. Meltay is unable to controvert ;
and I shall endeavour to keep only to such
parts of W. W.'s letter) that, directly a
society Man becomes an employer, he ceases
to be a member of our Society. W. W. has
therein penned a deliberate misrepresentation.
It is untrue. He knows that our rules allow
an employer to remain an ordinary member,
and fully entitled to benefit; or he can become
an honorary member, and if he should require
benefit he can make himself an ordinary
member again and be fully entitled to all
i
benefits in three months. It san absurd and
false stateinent "that a man might be a
society man (but for some reason, purely
imaginary) one day, and excluded the next,
mO.l &O." We, W. W.'s fellow members,
cannot understand the object of making such
false assertions. -W. W. plausibly and very
sophistically attempts to show that our trade
IS different from other trades, and that organi-
zation for mutual benefit is useless. What a
ridiculously false statement ; the more so,
ohm) W. W., twelve years ago, when working
for lower prices than at present, being
then in an inferior shop, and desirous of
bettering his position, made use of unity and
organisation for thatipurpose, and was one of the
foremost in advocating those means to reduce
the hours of labour. He also worked hard to
unite all branches of our trade, thereby form-
ing a Society which is at the present moment
an honour to us, and which I trust will be a
glory and a pattern to all other benevolent
Societies, for there is not one existing that has
adopted such impartial rules, and is so entirely
in the hands of us mechanics although; our
employers have liberally supported it yet they
have not any power within it. There is a
refutation from W. W's. own help, and I feel
sure he does .not regret the part he took in
forming that Society which from lack of unity
is not so powerful for good as it might be.
There is .no unity without discipline, the
simplest form of union is knowledge and. dis-
cipline to that extent; therefore, his remarks
about "the weakness of unity" are paradoxies,
and need no further comment. W. W. sus
"there arc plenty of young coachmakers who
etaud aloof from the nine hours' movement."
Unfortunately, hitherto, it is too true, for
reasons which would occupy too much space
for me to enter into, but one is, that such men
as W. W. get hold of a few young fellows and
persuade them that they are great authorities
upon political economy, &c., his remark sthereon
exhibiting an imbecility of thought surprising
in a young ooaohmaker like W. W. ; but
such expressions are scarcely to be wondered
at from one who characterises his
fellow workmen as second-rate London
swells. Did I not know W. W. I should have
been tempted to retort the "!Apeish " idea
Upon himself i but, "with all his faults I re-
spect him still," believing that he has allowed
himself to be mean the shield for designing
men, who are not altogether of our class, but,
who will most assuredly allow him to bear the
brunt of all the darts of scornful indignation,
'which will inevitably be hurled upon him.
Finally I ask W. W. whether such prices have
increased in consequence of us working a less
number of hours during the past five or say
20 years—for it is just 20 years ago this month
since the London coaohmakers hours were
reduced seven hours Per week, and six years
last February since we got the 4 o'clock on
Saturdays? I would also ask, whether those
London employers who took advantage of our
weakness—through slackness the year after—
to reduce the prices and day wages, if they,
since the great increase of trade during the
last two years (notwithstanding the increased
price of materials), have volunteered to raise
prices again I unhesistatingly Ban that under
the plea of having so much competition to deal
with, they, the London coaohbuilders, have
with glee reduced prices and wages; but
customers (of large firms, especially) have not
found the slightest difference unless it is in
inverse ratio—hence the large fortunes made
by those firms in a few years to the discom-
fiture of us, their mechanics, who have our-
selves to thank for not being united in one
strong phalanx, which would resist such
depredations upon individuals. Events are
" looming " which will force "senior members"
to bow to and fall into the advancing flood, so
that our ten paltry societies will adopt suoh
rulea,l that we shall be amalgamated in one
real United :Kingdom Society, which all the
leading spirits and statesmen of our age tell us
is essential to the general prosperity of every
trade, even as it is to society at large.
Apologising for troubling you at such length
and believing that W. W,'s letter will be an
incentive to enthusiasm in the good cause,-1
am, dr,o., EDWARD itRIiVELRY,
Coach-body Maker.
